Our analysis focuses on the duration of Abelian gauge fields in Einstein gravity, leveraging the metric tensor's symmetrized square of its contravariant components. By employing the covariant tensor representation and the post-Newtonian approximation, we derive the gauge field equations within the context of general relativity. Moreover, we demonstrate that the Fierz-pauli theory's consistency can be achieved through the application of Lorentzian group invariants to the second-order derivative coefficients of the perturbative equations.

This study examines a distributed regulation issue where a random evolution equation is used to model the evolution of a parameter. By reinterpreting the issue at hand through expected values, we demonstrate the exponential convergence of the parameter towards a predetermined equilibrium. Furthermore, we establish the existence of a feedback control policy that ensures the achievement of this goal in each possible scenario, resulting from the random parameters being specified.

Our research examined extremely extensive cosmic-ray networks observed at the Pierre Auger Observatory through the TOUGH criterion, which indicates the size and irregularity of these networks. We studied the characteristics of these networks in two areas with the observatory and compared them to the characteristics of individual air showers. Our findings show that the properties of the largest cosmic-ray networks exhibited significant fluctuations in both size and irregularity when compared to individual air showers. Furthermore, we found that the most irregular networks showed distinct properties when compared to the most extensive networks shown by other experiments. Our results also revealed that the most extensive and irregular networks exhibited distinct properties when compared to cosmic-ray showers of the same energy but detected through the SD criterion with the Telescope Array.
This paper proves that any alternative Zinbiel algebra automatically becomes a commutative algebra, which means it adheres to the characteristic of being a commutative algebra.

Our investigation focused on identifying and examining flow intensity and stream angle fluctuations in semi-central Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC's 5.02 TeV energy level. To achieve this, we employed an advanced technique known as the four-particle cumulant method, initially introduced by the ALICE collaboration. Following this approach, we calculated mean flow intensity values for particles aligned in specific directions within the collision plane. Next, we quantified flow fluctuations by calculating the correlation between stream angles and flow intensity. Our analysis revealed that initial geometry alone cannot fully explain flow fluctuations in semi-central collisions. Rather, we found that participant geometry underestimates flow fluctuations when compared to the standard 12% centrality gap. To fill in this gap, we proposed an innovative method based on the number of charged particles produced, which is calculable via simulations. Our analysis also compared flow fluctuations across different energy levels. In our research, flow fluctuations appeared consistent with predicted values based on buoyancy theory, which links fluctuations in initial density distributions within transverse planes of collisions. Furthermore, we found that flow fluctuations remained unchanged across different energy levels, even as average flow intensities showed significant increases with energy.

The process of comparing and merging data tables that contain identical structures but varying content is an essential task with numerous potential applications. It is crucial to integrate data from different sources in database integration, compare product catalogs across different websites, and match student data for college admissions. In these scenarios, two individual tables with the same structure are compared and merged into a single combined table. The comparison results in a new table that includes matched and unmatched data rows from the original tables, along with indications of their origins. The merge process also detects relationships between different data columns, specifically identifying instances where specific data columns are interconnected. In this research, we develop a method to manage discrepancies in tables that contain interconnected data columns, missing values, and functional relationships between the data. Along with the proposed algorithm, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to real-world data.

We introduce a novel time-varying point process model called TV-PAR, which leverages the power of self-adjusting parameters to capture changes in data trends. TV-PAR models enable efficient forecasting by utilizing past predictions as features, combined with machine learning-based temporal variation estimates. Unlike static PAR models that rely on stationary process assumptions, TV-PAR allows for predictions on models with non-stationary characteristics. Furthermore, TV-PAR models can adapt to temporal variations in data trends, ensuring accurate and utilization of historical data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of TV-PAR through comparative analysis of forecasting performance versus traditional models, showcasing improved results with time-varying parameters.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
incorporates both local and global information to enhance robustness to partial
observations and varying poses. NDFs comprise two main components: a set of
category-specific regional descriptors and a global neural network field without
category-specific information. We leverage the regional descriptors to capture
object features and the neural network field to model the probability distribution
of descriptors across all possible poses. In contrast to traditional methods that
depict this distribution through an explicit parameterized structure, we use a
latent latent grid that dynamically adapts to a pose-agnostic, uniform grid in
SE(3) space through the application of Normalizing Flows. This novel design
enables efficient and pose-conditioned sampling from the descriptor distribution.
Through rigorous evaluation on three diverse datasets involving object
recognition, segmentation, grasping, and manipulation, our NDF representation outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods across multiple metrics.

Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for O(N) universality classes in classical statistical mechanics. For model symmetry breaking, we have exact results for $N\geq 1$, showing the dimensionless coefficient $b_{\eta}$ equals $N$ for $d=1$, $N$ for $d=2$, $2$ for $d=3$ and $d-2$ for $d>3$. For the symmetry preserving case, we have new results for $N=1, N=2, N=4$ in $d=3$, and our previous result for $N=1$ in $d=2$. All results are for $h=2+k_{B}^{-4}\delta$ where $\delta$ represents a generic near-critical deviation from $h=0$.

In statistics and machine learning, an important problem is to reconstruct models from randomly distorted versions. To tackle this challenge, researchers rely on the second moment method. However, this approach requires a certain level of precision in the model reconstruction, which isn't always met due to the random noise used in the model's distortion. To make progress in this area, it would be helpful to have an estimate for the precision threshold that the noise must meet. Building on a recent advancement, we are able to provide such an estimate, which applies to a broader category of models than previously considered. Specifically, we examined a class of sparse models where the precision threshold the noise must meet is estimated to be around 10 times the current state-of-the-art limit, as indicated by a minimum of 10 precision thresholds in a representative dataset commonly used in research. We also demonstrated that the noise used in model reconstruction affects the precision threshold the noise must meet, which was not previously recognized. Furthermore, we found that the precision threshold the noise must meet can vary significantly, often unpredictably, with different noise used in model reconstruction, which was not previously known. These discoveries were made possible by a novel approach to estimating the precision threshold the noise must meet, which we introduced in a recent publication, and are relevant to a broader category of models than previously considered.

The monitoring of atmospheric aerosols has been made possible by using data from satellite photometry in multiple wavelengths. Recent studies have improved assessment methods to better account for various aerosol characteristics, optical behavior, and satellite measurement errors. These advancements include revised direct aerosol distribution retrieval methods, validation of existing models using extensive datasets, and research into the impact of model assumptions and satellite measurement limitations on aerosol analysis. Additionally, researchers have explored alternative approaches using evolutionary optimization, artificial neural networks, and traditional models, leading to enhanced accuracy in aerosol assessment. Furthermore, studies have been conducted to evaluate the validity of commonly applied models and algorithms, and to determine the optimal spatial scales for analyzing global aerosol distributions.

Advances in neural networks have led to significant improvements in estimating a object's pose using images, yet there are still challenges to be overcome, particularly for novel objects or those with complex configurations. To address this, we present DeepHMap++, a novel framework that tackles two major difficulties: correspondence and grouping, which are traditionally approached separately. Our method integrates correspondence and grouping into a single, unified process leveraging convolutional neural networks. In our architecture, correspondence and grouping are represented as competing objects in a single scene, which is then detected using a class-aware region proposal network. Testing DeepHMap++ on the LPD dataset shows promising results, with top performance among existing methods according to our evaluations. Furthermore, our method demonstrates versatility, displaying achievable results on the AIRHMAP dataset used for training aerial vehicles and an proxy experiment for novel objects.

We present GGLasso, a Python-based library for Generalized Graphical Lasso
techniques. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), we adapted the
algorithm to handle data with a non-identity covariance matrix. This is achieved
by transforming the data using the inverse covariance matrix, solving for the
graph, and then transforming it back to its original form. We explored two
methods for solving the inverse problem: using the Neumann series for small
graphs and a block-wise approach for larger, more complex graphs. Our tests
demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods along with the standard Graphical
Lasso approach. We also explored the relationship between the number of samples
and features required to recover a graph of a given sparsity. Our results show
that under certain conditions, we can recover a graph of size $n_{var} \times 50$
with just 500 samples.

Numerous numerical methods have been developed to model and simulate complex molecular systems, particularly those involving biomolecules. Despite significant advancements, many of these methods struggle with sampling high-dimensional configuration spaces efficiently, especially when comparing energies of similar and distinct phases. To compensate for slow exploration, researchers often rely on advanced techniques like barrier crossing methods or artificial intelligence, although there's a genuine need for more robust and straightforward strategies. Our proposal aims to provide a straightforward answer to this issue by combining the advantages of fast molecular dynamics simulations with rejection Monte Carlo, while introducing an auxiliary variable to improve the efficiency of configurational sampling. When applied to a model ring polymer, our method demonstrates enhanced exploration of the configuration space while maintaining fast dynamics. Additionally, our approach is effective at determining phase transitions in a simple Ising model.

Our research focuses on eigenvector-based methods to identify significant nodes in multi-layer networks. We examine the concept of eigenvector prominence, which measures a node's prominence across all network layers. This approach takes into account both the local connectivity and the significance of connected nodes. We found that the most prominent nodes in each layer are identical when networks are rearranged and renamed. Furthermore, we observed that the distribution of prominent nodes remains consistent when networks are altered, except in cases where there are significant changes in network connections. We analyzed multi-layer networks with varying levels of connection between different layers of the network and found that the results depend greatly on how the layers are connected. We also explored a wide range of power laws and non-uniform distributions of node significance within each network layer.

Recently, we generated a differential operator known as the Dirac operator within the $R$-Minkowski spacetime framework. Here, we derive the Dirac equation using this operator within the $R$-Minkowski spacetime context. Given that the metric within $R$-Minkowski spacetime is variable and complex, we reinterpret the physical meaning of the Dirac field's hermitian conjugate and gauge the symmetry group of the Dirac equation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the derived Dirac equation corresponds to a specific Hamiltonian within the $R$-Minkowski spacetime framework.

This study utilizes high-speed imaging to examine spheres interacting with a plane water surface, specifically in the moderate regime (0.5-3 m/s) where the seal response is most complex. A well-defined groove forms at the water surface as the spheres move through it, yet the seal area remains variable. An inconsistent pattern of ring formation is observed above the water surface, making it essential to ensure consistency in our analysis. This consistency is achieved by positioning the camera directly above the water surface, allowing us to study the seal response, ring pattern, and groove morphology for spheres of various sizes and different surface roughness. The results reveal that the spheres experience an initial sticking phase, during which the seal area is greatest, followed by a non-stick phase with an irregular ring pattern and varying seal area. The spheres' size affects the seal area in the non-stick phase, while surface roughness has a more significant impact on the ring pattern below the water surface. Furthermore, we identify three distinct patterns of ring formation: complete closure, partial closure with an arc-shaped ring, and no closure with a 360-degree ring. The factors influencing the seal response are closely tied to the fluid dynamics, particularly the formation of vortex streets above and below the water surface, which contribute to the complex behavior in the non-stick phase.

A well-known hypothesis posits that gravity at high-energy scales is characterized by a metric tensor alone, without any underlying symmetry other than general covariance. Under this assumption, a recent study developed a general framework for four-dimensional metric-independent effective field theories in Type IIB supergravity. The framework includes an effective action that is made up of three components: the gravitational sector, the $\theta$-term sector, and the gauge sector. The study found that the gauge sector must take on one of three possible forms: it can consist of a single Abelian $\theta$-term associated with a $U(1)_K$ gauge field, or it can consist of non-Abelian $\theta$-terms associated with either a single gauge field with self-coupling or multiple gauge fields with both self- and anti-self-coupling. The study found that even without assuming any specific gauge symmetry, the gauge sector can be expressed in a compact and symmetric form using a variety of non-trivial combinations of the $\theta$-term and Kähler-Dirac operator. The study also explored the possibility of extending the $\theta$-term sector to include the $\theta$-term of a chiral gravity multiplet in four-dimensional spacetime, which would lead to the generation of a negative cosmological constant. Our calculations using first-principles methods have demonstrated the unique
properties of cupricite, a rare mineral comprising copper and iron sulfides.
By comparing its results to those of monolayer cuprite and iron sulfide, we
have further elucidated its orbital-selective Mott behavior, which is influenced
by both electron--electron interactions and external electric field.
Our data indicate the presence of both localized and itinerant electrons in
cupricite, assigning its orbital-selective behavior as intermediate type.
Furthermore, our analysis of energy bands and density of states across its
orthorhombic monolayer structure have clarified the effects of lattice distortions
on its orbital-selective behavior; namely, that the t2g and eg orbitals, which
exhibit distinct distances from the Fermi energy, are symmetrically separated
along its unique crystallographic axes.
These findings are complemented by experimental data obtained using X-ray
absorption near edge structure and scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy
on a cupricite thin film, which has a similar orthorhombic monolayer structure.

A burgeoning field in quantum computing known as solid-state quantum optics with external fields lifted relies on intrinsic dipole moments to perform error-free two-qubit operations with minimal leakage. Here, we demonstrate immense Rabi oscillations between paired qubits situated in nearby Cp-like defects within a silicon surface layer. These defects exhibit strong coupling, in addition to an enormous electric dipole moment, and are remarkably resilient against phononic decoherence. Our calculations indicate that even without an external magnetic field, the nearest neighbor qubit pair can be programmed to execute intricate algorithms on one qubit while keeping the other unchanged, exceeding the record for binary rotations executed with minimal error within silicon.

Our investigation focused on an intriguing two-dimensional non-symmorphic wallpaper structure, featuring a unique combination of glide reflection symmetries and kissing lattices. To analyze this structure's electronic properties, we employed a combination of group theoretical and tight-binding methods. Our results revealed the existence of Dirac points within the non-symmetric momentum range and the possibility of adjusting their number and location through external applied pressure. Our study also compared the structure's properties to a two-dimensional kagome lattice, revealing distinct differences in their electronic feature spectra.

Quantum states known as single-photon facilitated coherent states (SPFCS) possess the ability to store multiple photons within a beam, only releasing them in response to a specific photon being detected. This property makes SPFCS suitable for providing a basis for quantum computation through the use of a controlled release of a photon, followed by a subsequent coherent state restoration. We examine the parameters influence on the quantum properties of SPFCS generated through quantum-optical catalysis using a beam splitter and a photon box. Furthermore, we investigate the effectiveness of this state in emitting multiple photons in a sequence detected upon losing the beam's stability, along with the effectiveness of coherent state restoration following a single-photon detection.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the Weyl conformal curvature tensor and its associated operators. Beginning with an assumption that the Einstein field equation holds, we determine the bivector coefficients which satisfy the Einstein field equation, thus determining the solutions to Einstein's field equation within the Newman-Penrose formalism.

The lack of efficient data-driven methods for developing polymers is a significant challenge, which our technique aims to address. Our approach leverages experimental data to build predictive models of physical properties using linear regression, followed by an integer optimization algorithm to select suitable monomers and their proportions in a polymer. We demonstrate the potential of this approach by applying it to our dataset of copolymers.

We present a novel medical image segmentation technique based on dense attention and unet architectures, known as DDAUnet, which effectively distinguishes and highlights crucial points for accurate segmentation. This technique comprises two distinct attention mechanisms that pinpoint critical pixels for each pixel, as well as a dense attention module that determines the importance of neighboring pixels. In addition to these mechanisms, we extracted and incorporated valuable semantic information from distant image regions to enhance segmentation performance. Our DDAUnet model was applied to the manual annotation avoidance in esophageal tumor segmentation from CT scans, yielding a Jaccard index of 0.61, a Dice coefficient of 0.75, and a mean surface distance of 5.08mm in a publicly available dataset.

Code-mixed languages, which combine two or more languages in a document, are a result of bilingual communication and are used for convenience and better expression. This practice is observed across social media platforms and is particularly prevalent among multilingual communities. Code-mixed language models on the other hand have not seen the same level of development as monolingual models despite the abundance of available data. This paper explores the reasons behind this discrepancy and highlights the intricate challenges and complexities of model development in this domain. It also examines the limited range of code-mixed models and the restricted scope of applications they support. Notably, research on code-mixed models often focuses on individual tasks and genres of data rather than comprehensive, multi-task, and cross-genre problems. Moreover, codemixed models often mirror the characteristics of their corresponding monolingual models, with little consideration for the unique aspects of code-mixed language. This paper also delves into the distinct features of code-mixed language, the problems codemixed models encounter, and the little progress made in addressing the intricate issues of multilingual codemixed models.

The metric used to evaluate image description systems is continuously evolving,
driven by improvements in computer vision and neural language processing.
Describing images that are dissimilar requires a more nuanced method,
one that distinguishes between visually dissimilar images and those with
different reference annotations.
Our analysis includes a proposal for a new description assessment metric,
the diverse description metric (DDM), which gauges the system's ability
to generate accurate descriptions for visually dissimilar images and those
with diverse references.
Our experiments involve a large-scale dataset with diverse references
and demonstrate the benefits of of DDM over existing metrics.

Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values, minimal reflectivity, and transparent conductivity. As a result of their versatile electronic structure, ranging from insulating to conducting phases, Ta$_2$O$_5$ compounds are highly desirable for use in optical devices, semiconductor interfaces, and memristor applications. Nevertheless, their material properties are sensitive to defects, interfaces, and oxygen deficiencies. Notwithstanding this sensitivity, theoretical modeling of their properties is challenging due to uncertainties in their crystal structure. At room temperature, Ta$_2$O$_5$ compounds exhibit a complex, anisotropic behavior resulting from multiple phases and structures, including the alpha, beta, and gamma phases, in addition to polyoxo-metalate structures. In this study, we explored the possible phases and structures of Ta$_2$O$_5$ through ab-initio and Monte Carlo simulations, focusing on the base state crystal structure and electronic properties. By examining the energy vs. cell volume of various phases and structures, we identified the most stable phases corresponding to different oxygen contents, and compared our results with experimental data on the phases and structures of Ta$_2$O$_5$ compounds.

Previous studies attributed the Big Geographic Sort, referring to the tendency for similar people to be physically separated from those who are dissimilar, to be primarily a result of cultural transmission. In this study, we investigate the Big Geographic Sort's impact on the spread of misinformation. Utilizing Reddit data and a method to measure geographic sorting at the individual level, we found that individuals who exhibit greater geographic sorting tend to engage in less social reference, including fact-checking, with their physically distant peers. Furthermore, we detected an association between the Big Geographic Sort and the dissemination of misinformation. Specifically, we found that misinformation spreads more easily among those who exhibit greater geographic sorting, particularly among those with a conservative online profile.

Humans use sound patterns emitted from their own bodies to convey important information to other people. Although previously overlooked, considering these intrinsic sounds as part of social communication is vital, especially in controlled environments like training and instruction. Research has shown that humans process auditory feedback from robots effectively, but the role of intrinsic human sounds in these interactions remains unknown. This study investigates how the sounds produced by humans, specifically their voice and bodily noises, affect the understanding of instructions given to a robot in a training setting. The findings reveal that the sounds produced by humans, other than their voice, are generally irrelevant background noise, but the sounds associated with their actions, like scraping sounds, enhance comprehension by drawing attention to the relevant task element. This effect is more pronounced when the sound is produced near the robot's workspace. Notably, the presence of these sounds also influences the preference for robot instructions that include demonstration versus just verbal guidance. This study's results have implications for the design of sound-enhanced robot instructions that incorporate intrinsic human sounds to facilitate comprehension and preference in various work environments.

A new framework for describing conformal field theory complexity has been established in (arXiv: 2105.04470, arXiv: 2105.04472). Within this context, a set of nonlinear Euler-Arnold equations serves as a characteristic signature of complexity, whose specific form is determined by a universal, physically-prefixed parameter. This prefixed parameter manifests as a scalar value in d dimensions, which we have found to be directly linked to the proportionality constant in the fundamental complexity evolution equation. Furthermore, in the course of our earlier studies, particularly in arXiv: 2105.04472, we demonstrated that a particular class of solvable lattice operators could be effectively represented as a complex operator in a d-dimensional space, with specific properties. Here, we expand on this insight by revealing that the lattice operator's intrinsic characteristics, including its asymptotic behavior, geometric structure, and interactions, can be interpreted through the lens of conformal field theory in (1+1)D. Notably, our findings related to the Euler-Arnold equations hold universally, without dependence on the specific d-dimensional space in which the operator is defined.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and the demand for high-quality dialog systems is rising. While there are established methods for training and evaluating single models in tasks like text classification and generation, machine teaching for dialog systems differs significantly due to their intricate structure and the dynamic nature of user interactions. In response to these challenges, we propose a novel evaluation framework centered on user behavior rather than system responses. We believe this approach provides a fair and relevant assessment of dialog systems' performance and detection of flaws. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through a user study and a critical examination of Amazon Mechanical Turk's crowdsourcing. We also introduce a cost-efficient strategy for selecting relevant user interactions. Notably, our approach is applicable to various dialog systems, and we show this consistency with a publicly available bot.

Cross-domain recommendation has been a highly sought-after topic in recent years, as it enables the effective utilization of data from related domains. However, multi-sparse-domain settings pose a significant challenge due to the abundance of domains and items within them. Current methods primarily focus on using attribute preference or comprehensive learning, but these often fall short due to sparse data across domains. To address this, we propose a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR) that leverages cooperative attribute preference and comprehensive learning. In this framework, we first build a robust attribute preference network for each item category using meta-learning, and then integrate a cooperative comprehensive network that shares knowledge across domains. The evaluation of MSDCR using real-world data from the Amazon dataset shows promising results, with a notable improvement over existing methods across multiple metrics.

Conic optimization is a highly effective tool for solving a wide range of problems, leveraging the versatility of conic structures that reflect problem characteristics. As such conic models are derived from real-world applications, solving their duals can lead to complex and non-smooth problems. To address this, we propose an alternative framework based on the concept of conic representations, which bypasses the dualization process. This approach allows us to work directly with the original conic expressions and their underlying structures, enabling efficient computation of subgradients. We demonstrate the utility of this method by applying it to the specific task of solving stochastic differential games, where we derive a new algorithm tailored to this domain. We also make available a Julia package, Hypatia, which implements these methods and provides users with an interface for defining conic expressions and their corresponding structures, as well as solving algorithms tailored to various contexts.

The escalating use and complexity of MRI systems have made quality assurance a pressing concern for medical imaging, with institutional standards varying widely. As a result, developing a standardized quality metric that accounts for multiple variables, such as multiple institutions and imaging protocols, has become increasingly vital. We addressed this challenge by constructing an institutional QA system and a protocol QA system and then evaluated their effectiveness using real data from multiple sources. Our research revealed that a one-institution QA system struggles to accurately rate images from a different institution, with a score difference of up to 20%. Conversely, a one-protocol QA system successfully differentiates images acquired from either of of two similar protocols with near-perfect accuracy, and slightly lower accuracy for two protocols with some degree of similarity. Additionally, we discovered a disconnection between clinical ratings and quantitative QA scores, with a correlation of just 20%. We concluded that developing a universal QA system is not feasible given the current institutional standards, with over 90% showing unique characteristics. Therefore, the most effective approach is to develop an institution-specific QA system, tailored to their unique parameters and standards.

To understand the impact of private electric vehicles on power grid resilience, a comprehensive study is necessary. Utilizing a proposed management framework that combines intelligent transportation systems and energy management systems as reference frameworks, we broke down the individual components to better analyze their effects. We examined the influences of private EVs on power consumption, generation, and grid stability through various scenarios. Our findings indicate that private EVs have the potential to improve grid stability in some areas but may jeopardize overall resilience in others. Our research demonstrates that private EVs' distinct charging habits hold significant predictive value, allowing for targeted policy interventions to enhance grid resilience. We propose a private EV classification system that divides vehicles into three categories based on their owners' behavior: those who charge during off-peak hours, those who prioritize vehicle use over charging, and those who prioritize charging over vehicle use. We also developed a decision-making framework that leverages multi-agent optimization to mitigate potential disruptions and demonstrated its efficacy with a real-world data set from Changsha, China.

In multi-agent meetings, participants share information and work together
to achieve shared goals by motivating and directing each other. To effectively
capture the complex dynamics of such meetings, we introduce a novel framework
based on incentive theory and drive-based models. Within this framework, we
propose the MIRD framework, which combines mechanisms that motivate and drive
actions. The MIRD framework consists of two main components: a drive network
that represents action preferences and a mechanism network that provides incentives
based on shared goals. The drive network and mechanism network are separate and
can be safely set to the same value of interest. We prove that under certain
conditions, the drive network and mechanism network converge to the same value.
To demonstrate the practical applications of the MIRD framework, we use it
to simulate meetings between agents working towards shared goals and show that it
outperforms the current state-of-the-art method.

This paper examines the fundamental characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 using computational methods. The optimization of their crystal structure, analysis of their electronic and magnetic properties were investigated using the GGA+U method. The results show that the crystal structure of these compounds has a cubic space group 225, with all atoms located at the 8c lattice site. The calculation of their lattice parameter and bulk modulus yielded values close to the available experimental data. The band structure and density of states revealed that these compounds possess a direct indirect bandgap. The magnetic properties indicated all compounds have a ferromagnetic nature with a high spin moment. The calculations of their total magnetic moment and lattice magnetic moment showed they behave similarly to each other. Notably, the total magnetic moment remains constant at 3μB per formula unit across the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, demonstrating these compounds exhibit excellent stability in their magnetic properties.

Based on quark combination models, researchers are forecasting the existence of exotic baryons and mesons that have yet to be observed. These predictions envision a vast spectrum of particles across the mass range, from a few hundred MeV to several GeV. Although the QCD cascade will likely obscure many of these particles, neutrino and photon probes may enquire about their existence in high-energy collisions. This work is a follow-up to Danilov et al., but with a broader scope, covering a more extensive array of quark configurations and combining chiral and non-chiral combinations of quarks. As a result, predictions for mesons and baryons become more extensive, with some combinations even anticipating the existence of glueballs and Higgs-like particles.

The concept of root subgroups in the classical Chevalley groups over a given field has a significant implications for the structure and properties of these groups. A fundamental theorem by the mathematicians Shoji and Hagiwara establishes relationships between the conjugating operators of these root subgroups within the symmetric groups and the Coxeter groups of type B, and they prove the conjugating operators are rational functions that contain only even powers of the variable x. In this study, we provide a generalization of the mentioned theorem, discovering that the conjugating operators for the classical Chevalley groups over a field with an odd characteristic contain powers of x with a specific parity, which is determined based on the n-fold duals of a polynomial called the Frobisher invariant.

We re-examined the relationship between the distribution of lensing magnifications and the properties of Type Ia supernovae using the Pantheon sample and a model with a Gaussian distribution of mass perturbations within galaxies. Calculating the cross-sections for lensing deflections and the associated optical depths, we found the probability of a lensing event by a single galaxy to be approximately 0.007 for a mass range of $10^{11.5}-10^{12.5} M_{\odot}$. Allowing for the overlap of galaxies within the field of view, we calculated the total optical depth for a sample of supernovae and found it to be $\approx 0.25$ for a mass range of $10^{11.5}-10^{13.5} M_{\odot}$. We compared our results to previous studies, particularly Wambsganss (1995), and found the optical depth to be in agreement with the latter, with a narrower mass range. A novel type of T-shaped junction (T hub) was successfully created within a silicon-on-insulator photonic material. Scanning near-field optical microscopy was utilized to examine the T hub's near-field properties and behavior at the microscale. Contrary to expectations, we discovered that T hubs exhibit a unique characteristic: instead of generating a strong focus of light, they produce a light distribution pattern similar to that found within dielectric microresonators. As a result, T hubs can be viewed as a primitive form of microresonators and may have applications in the near-field enhancement of optical signals within photonic devices.

Context-aware object recognition is a key functionality for machines that are perceiving and interpreting visual environments. Researchers have made significant progress in recognizing individual objects within images, yet the task of integrating this knowledge to identify the context of objects within a scene remains a challenge. The paper proposes an innovative method for evaluating the context of objects using deep learning recognizers, which considers the spatial relationships among objects within a scene. The proposed assessment metric relies on training a suite of context-modified object recognizers and uses the differences between these recognizers and a individual object recognizer as an indicator of the context's impact. The paper also recommends a suite of scenarios for evaluating the context of objects within scenes that are both real-world and synthetic. Real-world scenarios were derived from existing datasets for context-aware object recognition, such as CARS and FogBank, which comprise images depicting multiple objects and complex relationships. Synthetic scenarios were created using a generator for scene synthesis, along with a score for context complexity. The paper presents multiple experiments using these datasets and scenarios to demonstrate the practical applications of the proposed assessment metric.

We have derived several important inequalities, including the Kirchhoff type singular elliptic system, the multiple Trudinger-Moser inequality, and the Ambrosetti-Baldi-Calami inequality, which are significant in the study of partial differential equations. These inequalities have been established under either multiple concavity or volume growth conditions. Our main result demonstrates that there exists a multiplicity of solutions to the Kirchhoff type singular elliptic system under either one of the following conditions: either $n<8$, the space has the property of infinite volume growth, or the space has a specific structure with infinite volume.

We establish concentration inequalities for sums of dependent binary random variables with negative correlation, specifically those based on the Tsutsui-Russo and Buhlmann aggregating schemes, as well as weighted averages of such variables. These inequalities result in tail bounds for the individual variables, which in the case of the Tsutsui-Russo scheme yields an exponential bound with a weakly increasing dependence on the number of variables, while the Buhlmann scheme leads to a log-linear bound in the number of variables.

We establish a key connection between the charted symplectic transformation group and the symplectic transformation group through the concept of a generating system of functions, which are pairwise compositionally invariant under the given alteration. By leveraging the Darboux theorem and the inverse function theorem, we demonstrate that any symplectic transformation can be expressed as a product of an arbitrary number of charted transformations associated with specific alterations, which are termed compositionally generic. It is noteworthy that all compositionally generic alterations can be linked to a specific alteration when they are linked through continuous paths.

The suitability of kidneys for transplantation is evaluated on a case-by-case
basis, with medical professionals using their discretion to make judgments.
Studies have shown that, in the past, female kidneys were less desirable for
transplantation due to concerns about donor height and weight, despite being
biologically identical to male kidneys. With the increase in donor shortages
and improved transplant outcomes, the selection criteria for kidneys has
became more flexible. This paper examines issues related to the selection of
kidneys, particularly those resulting from incompatible pairs, and discusses the
ideal acceptance criteria for such organs. By considering the perspectives
and values of transplant recipients, donors, and their families, as well as the
ethical implications of donation, we argue that an ideal acceptance policy
should prioritize the utilization of donated kidneys over other considerations.

Recent studies using word representations in financial text analysis have been questioned about their effectiveness, specifically concerns have been raised that they may overfit the original data, leading to poor performance when transferred to new, similar domains. Another area of concern involves word representations and emotional language, specifically with the Common Word Embedding Theorem that posits word representations are directly linked to word frequencies. However, a critique of this assumption has been presented by Loughran and McDonald, who argue that word representations neglect the grammatical function of words, which influences their emotional content. In this research, we re-examine the claim made by Loughran and McDonald that word representations fail to capture the grammatical function of words, which in turn affects their emotional content. We achieve this by re-examining adjectival and adverbial polarities presented in their original study and find that their results are influenced by incorrect assumptions or statistical flaws. As a result, we are unable to support the claim made by Loughran and McDonald. A closer examination of their methods also yields an alternative polarity calculation, which we believe accurately captures the emotional content of words, including their grammatical function.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based alternatives for a previous study on wideband waveforming by integrated transmitters and receivers. The previous study demonstrated how waveforming can provide an additional benefit in the form of increased data transfer rates beyond multiple antennas and carrier aggregation. The SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based approaches can be seen as variants of the original idea and the previous study's results will be shown as natural extensions to these variants.

This research introduces a new method to model the boundary between two fluids with different properties, such as a interface between a solid and a melting phase. Based on the conservation equations for fluid dynamics, it uses a level-set and embedded boundary method, combining the advantages of both approaches to solve problems like phase change, surface tension, and melting ice. A blend of the conservative and non-conservative level-set methods is used to model the flow, and a discrete surface tension force is calculated to replicate the physical behavior. This approach enables the representation of complex boundary conditions and surface phenomena within the level-set framework.

In multiagent competitions, players facing unknown opponents often learn
strategies through trial and error. To optimize their performance, they
typically rely on data-driven method learning from experience. In this study,
we focus on settings where players act rationally, choosing actions that
maximize their payoff based on observed information. We developed an algorithm
called "exploiting contextual rationalizability" or ECR for short, which uses
contextual multiarmed bandits to efficiently find a rationalizable equilibrium
by analyzing the data from past interactions. We established the regret of ECR
is controlled by a factor of $\sqrt{dT}\ln(T)$ when learning alone and $\sqrt{T}(\sqrt{k}+d\sqrt{K})\ln(T)$ in multiagent competitions, 
improving the existing results in the literature.

In this study, a SIR model with preventive mitigation measures such as travel restrictions and social distancing is proposed to better understand the spread of epidemics within various networks. Initially, the model consists of separate Ising models for individuals who follow restrictions and those who do not, with an energy difference defined by an epidermic parameter. As the parameter decreases in value, the model shifts from a disordered state to an ordered state through a critical point. Through probabilistic methods and analysis of a discrete time model, the disordered state's characteristics are examined, particularly the probability that an individual remains healthy or infected. Additionally, the model's dynamics and network effects on the model's behavior, specifically around the critical point, are explored in simulations of good quality.

Our proposed framework simplifies the complex relationships between datasets, theoretical predictions, and parton distribution functions (PDFs) by treating PDFs as variables influencing theoretical predictions, rather than targets. This shift in perspective allows us to treat PDFs as variables that need to be adjusted to match measured data, a approach identical to the traditional method of fitting PDFs to data. Our framework maintains the same level of information as the original formulation and is thus fully equivalent. However, this new perspective offers several practical benefits, including the practicality of treating PDFs at different energies as variables in data fitting, and the potential to develop novel algorithms for fitting PDFs.

To improve the effectiveness of experience replay, we propose a novel scheme
to select data for policy optimization by minimizing the variance of the
estimated policy loss. This variance estimation is critical for guiding the
sampling process, as it enables our method to efficiently explore the most
informative data, thereby, significantly reducing policy loss estimation
variance. As a result, our method yields superior performance, surpassing both
random experience replay and prioritized experience replay by a margin of
20% and 30% respectively, when applied to challenging benchmark tasks in
robotic grasping and navigation. Furthermore, our method demonstrates the
ability to accelerate policy optimization without relying on hyperparameter
tuning, as it is inherently robust to various sampling ratio configurations.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of diversity (11 ways to measure) through our specially 
designed selection process. These dialogues exhibit varied characteristics such 
as alternating turns, diverging topics, different speaker roles, list or tree-like 
structures, and more. By leveraging the 128-task graph we introduced in our previous 
work, the MultiTalk Dataset offers multiple dialogue continuation challenges, along 
with an assessment of our dialogue generation model using an expanded version of 
the Dynamic Dialogue Evaluation Framework.

We present a series of 64 N-body simulations for a conformally coupled gravity model, where the sum of matter densities is kept constant, using a new code developed in Python. These simulations modeled the evolution of an irrotational, dark matter-dominated universe with an initial perturbation, and were highly efficient, completing 64 simulations in less than 30 minutes on a single core. Our results for the power spectra of density fluctuations are consistent with previous findings, but our analysis went further in comparing the characteristics of initial conditions that lead to the formation of galaxies in this altered gravity scenario. We found that the power spectra of the unique modes of density fluctuations that grow in this scenario are distinct, especially at high k values, potentially serving as a distinguishing feature for future galaxy surveys within a Hubble volume.

A recent theory posits that any chordal loopted SLE in genus greater than zero can be extended to a wide family of whole-plane loopted Schramm-Loewner evolutions, across a specific graph of finite depth. According to this framework, we demonstrate that there exists a universal way to enlarge chordal SLE in the hyperbolic plane to a whole-plane definition, and this whole-plane version is characterized by a specific parameterization of driving functions. The characterization involves linking the whole-plane version to a random field defined on the unit disk, which is composed of multiple Gaussian free fields, and it also drives whole-plane SLE through a process that generalizes the relationship between subdomain SLE and the Gaussian free field within that subdomain. The whole-plane whole-line SLE is further shown to be equivalent to a specific random log-gas within the real line, and its whole-plane version driven by this log-gas is characterized by a specific parameterization of driving functions. Both characterizations are novel contributions of this study.

MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source, open-data platform based on MediaWiki's source code and data structure, intended for the development of custom knowledge-building projects. Building upon the underlying architecture of Wikipedia, WorkingWiki provides a starting point for creating tailored collaborative environments, with features like user management, page revisions, and a search engine. The project specifically addresses the needs of research groups working together, with features like page and file permissions, email updates, and the ability to upload files with automated metadata. Furthermore, WorkingWiki is highly customizable through its PHP and MySQL interfaces, with extensions and templates at users' disposal. As an example of WorkingWiki's potential, the project includes the source code and data structure for the ASL Wiki project, an accessible language research database.

A linearized model is developed to study the acoustic properties of turbulent jet fires. The model utilizes a linearized active flame model, which separates the acoustics and chemistry solutions, and is based on an active flame approach. The model assumes a stable flame and does not rely on global stability analysis. It includes an expression for flame speed that is independent of distance, as well as an expression that connects the flame speed with the mean flow properties. To validate the model, results from direct numerical simulations of a jet fire were compared with the model's predictions, showing good agreement. The model also successfully predicted the effects of acoustic forcing on a jet fire in a linearized framework.

We investigate the impact of neutrinos interacting with ultralight dark matter on the $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay and cosmological parameters. Assuming that neutrinos have a non-zero mass and that the dark matter is ultralight with a mass similar to the neutrino mass, we consider interactions mediated by a light vector boson with conserved charge. By analyzing four scenarios of neutrino mass hierarchies, we determine the minimal dark matter density required to accommodate the heaviest neutrino mass within the Arbesbach et al. limit. Consequently, this limit is strengthened to $|g_{\rm A}^{\rm V}/g_{\rm A}^{\rm S}| \lesssim 10^{-3}$ for a vector boson with a mass in the $10^{-25}$eV range. Furthermore, we find that the dark matter density is directly proportional to the square of the light vector boson mass, and its impact on the $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay is modified to be in line with the nuclear matrix element. Additionally, we determine the dark matter density constraints from the CMB and large-scale structure data within the effective field theory framework, which are in agreement with previous findings.

We introduce a novel nonlocal gravity theory, based on an intrinsic metric-free approach, where the nonlocal connection is defined through an invertible propagator in the frequency domain. By postulating that the nonlocal connection can be described by an invertible operator in the frequency domain, we derive the nonlocal gravity theory equations in the spacetime domain. A key aspect of this approach is the use of an overcomplete basis of tetrads, which allows for the derivation of the nonlocal gravity theory equations in the spacetime domain. We show that the nonlocal gravity theory equations can be obtained using a variational approach, by postulating that the nonlocal connection can be described by an invertible operator in the frequency domain. We also show that the nonlocal gravity theory equations can be obtained using a variational approach, by postulating that the nonlocal connection can be described by an invertible operator in the frequency domain. We further show that the nonlocal gravity theory equations can be obtained using a variational approach, by postulating that the nonlocal connection can be described by an invertible operator in the frequency domain. We also show that the nonlocal gravity theory equations can be obtained using a variational approach, by postulating that the nonlocal connection can be described by an invertible operator in the frequency domain.
