A detailed investigation of the Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem reveals its consistency by applying it to both relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theories. The analysis demonstrates the theorem's accuracy within the symmetries that characterize the spinless NG bosons. However, in the nonrelativistic context, the theorem is revised to better suit the symplectic nature of the phase space. As a result, the corrected theorem indicates that the absence of a full set of commuting number and creation operators within the spinless NG boson sector leads to the generation of masses for bosons and fermions. Consequently, this effect causes the NG mode to become a massive scalar or Dirac particle instead of a massless mode. Furthermore, the phenomenon is exemplified through the symmetry breaking scenarios of $\phi^3$ and $\phi^4$ theories within both the relativistic and nonrelativistic frameworks.

Our proposed method, called Discriminative Counterfactual Selection Model (DISCO), leverages the power of large language models to create phrasal counterfactuals that contradict a given sentence. To demonstrate the versatility of our approach, we show that a single LLM can be used to generate diverse counterfactuals for any input sentence by prioritizing unlikely outcomes. Our analysis reveals that generated counterfactuals are sensible and rare occurrences, occurring in approximately 1% of all possible outcomes. By examining the LLM's structural properties, we discover that it effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect counterfactuals by relying on semantic differences rather than frequency-based distinctions. To validate our method, we use an LLM to create counterfactuals for multiple sentence pairs and discover a 24% improvement in the task accuracy over a frequentist approach. Moreover, we integrate an LLM into an existing process for training counterfactual-exposing models and discover a 5-fold decrease in required training examples.

The surface energy of substrates plays a significant role in surface science, particularly through remote epitaxy, where it facilitates film growth at a distance. We investigated the equilibrium between remote epitaxy, van der Waals epitaxy, and pinhole epitaxy on a single substrate - graphene on alpha-Al2O3. By developing a free energy model, we found that a critical misfit dislocation density exists, below which remote epitaxy dominates over van der Waals epitaxy, and this could be experimentally verified through high-resolution transmission electron microscopy. Moreover, we established that remote epitaxy is favored on flat graphene surfaces due to misfit dislocation segregation at graphene/sapphire defects. Notably, by controlling defects within the graphene layer, it is possible to switch between these growth equilibria, making this system extremely versatile for developing multifunctional van der Waals heterostructures.

A code is called $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a specific type of encoding process called the Gray image of codes that have properties under the $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-module structure. In our study, we examine the dimension of these codes and identify those with a dual that have maximal distance. Notably, this work extends and complements the findings related to the dimension of $\Z_p$-linear codes and their duals with a maximal distance for even $p$.

Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific instances that fulfill multiple conditions. However, most current methods focus solely on training models for a single label instance generation task at a time, without considering multi-label situations. A major limitation of existing approaches becomes apparent - they do not address multi-label instance generation. Our proposed framework, MGNet, breaks ground by leveraging the potential of conditional GANs for multi-label instance generation. MGNet generates models that can produce instances labeled with multiple classes, not just a single class. The network's unique design enables the generation of complex datasets as the condition is defined as a simple linear operation. We evaluate MGNet on multiple datasets and present comparative results with current methods, demonstrating its superior performance.

Quantum systems can be modeled using mathematical structures known as Dirac structures, particularly within the framework of dagger compact closed categories. Given two such systems, defined as input and output objects within a graph, there exists a well-defined Poisson bracket that characterizes the evolution of physical observables. The relationship between these systems can be captured through morphisms within the category, specifically when the graph contains a loop. When the graph consists of a single loop, these morphisms are associated with the symplectic leaves of the Poisson bracket. To extend this relationship to more complex systems involving multiple loops, one must consider the relationship between the associated symplectic leaves. This task can be achieved by mapping the input and output objects to Hilbert spaces and utilizing the associated operators to return to the original systems, effectively mapping the systems to their equivalent within the category. This process is facilitated by utilizing the properties of dagger compact closed categories, specifically the ability to convert between objects and morphisms, as well as the relationship between operators and systems. Notably, this process involves utilizing the properties of the graph, particularly the loops, to define the operator corresponding to each object within the system.

The exact origin of gamma-rays above 50 TeV in the nearby BL Lac type gamma-ray blazars remains a mystery. To tackle this challenge, we examine two popular models for high-energy photon production – synchrotron radiation from electrons within a bright jet component and external Comptonization – using extensive simulations and energy spectra calculations. We calculate the energy spectra of electrons required for the synchrotron radiation model and find that they lead to unrealistic results, particularly in some blazars, due to the excessive production of high-energy photons above 10 TeV. In contrast, the external Comptonization model produces more plausible results. We also consider a previously unaccounted source of electrons – magnetic fields within the surrounding environments of active galaxies – which can give rise to captured disks affecting the surrounding space. We calculate the energy spectra of electrons in the jet components and the high-energy photon spectra in the surrounding space, finding that they match observed data in some blazars. We propose that the captured disks in the surrounding environments of active galaxies can account for the high-energy gamma-rays observed in some nearby BL Lac type gamma-ray blazars.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial and methods like machine learning on phonocardiogram sounds can provide valuable insights, though their efficacy depends on the quality of recorded sounds. In clinical settings, recorded sounds are often distorted by electrical interference and mechanical noise from beds, which can hinder the effectiveness of these methods. To mimic real-world recording conditions and explore method effectiveness, researchers typically add white Gaussian noise to sound recordings. However, such noise additions do not accurately represent actual recording environments. To bridge this gap, researchers propose a new protocol that includes both Gaussian noise and convolutional noise model simulations to mimic real recordings more accurately. Additionally, they introduce a novel approach that leverages cyclical transformations to describe the complex dynamics evident in heart sounds. To demonstrate the practical value of this protocol, they conduct multiple machine learning-based heart sound category classification experiments using data generated according to their protocol. Compared to standard protocols, the new approach yields superior performance results, thereby validating the proposed methodology.

The proliferation of wearable devices for health monitoring has created a vast amount of data, presenting a potential resource for developing sophisticated, data-driven medical applications. However, training accurate models using wearable data from diverse sources is challenging due to variations in data quality, quantity, and characteristics across these sources. In this paper, a pioneering federated transfer learning approach is presented for developing medical models using wearable data. In this framework, an initial model is trained on data from a smaller, representative cohort before being fine-tuned on a larger, more diverse dataset across multiple sources. The proposed method, FedHealth, leverages personalized models trained on individual data sources and combines them using a federated approach, enabling efficient development of medical applications across various settings. Experimental evaluations using real data from multiple sources, along with simulated data sets, demonstrate the efficacy of FedHealth in comparison to conventional approaches.

This study compares and contrasts portfolio optimization strategies that build on stochastic programming, robust optimization, two-stage robust optimization, and two-stage robust optimization with information sharing. We break down the intricacies of these methods through a standard mean-variance framework, highlighting the implications for portfolio performance and risk management. A numerical example and an empirical analysis using stocks listed on the Kolm index provide empirical evidence for the theoretical findings. The study's outcomes reveal that across various scenarios, changing from classical to advanced methods does not necessarily lead to increased risk or decreased performance. Interestingly, some scenarios show the opposite effect, albeit anxiolytic when considered in the context of the estimated standard error. The study's duration was two months, covering January to February 2020, based on daily data.

The rise of cloud-native technologies, coupled with expanding automation
trends across the software development life cycle, have resulted in increasingly
complex software systems being developed at an accelerated pace. As a result,
testing and validation tasks have grown in scope, complexity, and time
requirements, necessitating innovative automated testing methods. In response to
these challenges, the interest has grown in the area of model-based testing,
leading to an increase in research focused on applying and developing own
technologies, rather than a one-size-fits-all approach. At the same time, there
is an expanding need to consider human elements in the development of testing
strategies, going beyond the purely technical aspects of testing.

This study examines a stochastic control problem characterized by the goal of maximizing expected terminal wealth under risk, subject to constraints on the total cost of controls that can grow infinitely as they become more erratic. To approach this problem, we develop a new asset allocation strategy involving the toggling of risk assets for bonds in a discrete time Markovian autoregressive model. Through this method, we contain the total cost of controls at the cost of a stationary distribution of discrete time Markovian autoregressive processes. Consequently, this yields a dual objective of maximizing the expected terminal payoff under risk, subject to constraints on the sum of the costs of controls and a new measure that represents the distance between the terminal wealth and the stationary distribution. We further show that the optimal policy is deterministic, enabling the computation of its features through the verification theorem of its Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs system. Additionally, we provide a closed-form solution for a special case.

A novel approach is presented for discovering leptoquark pairs with unequal masses, utilizing the collision data from the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The proposed method involves examining signals from the collision of protons with 13 TeV energy and 139 inverse femtobarns of integrated luminosity. The research focuses on identifying leptoquark pairs with charges that differ by at least half a unit, making some predictions about how they would interact and suggesting various interaction types are unlikely. The likely sources of these leptoquark pairs are abnormal neutrino interactions or unusual properties of protons. A range of predictions is made for both first- and second-generation leptoquark pairs, with expectations for finding first-generation pairs with masses between 0.94 and 1.28 TeV or second-generation pairs with masses between 0.85 and 1.16 TeV. A proposed method for finding these pairs is also described, along with expected results for both the CMS and ATLAS experiments.

We analyze the influence of external radiation stimulating fine structure lines, particularly the 15647 \ Å line of C I, on molecular gas within galaxies. To assess this effect, we compare observations from the HERA and ALMA at 6 \ Å and 254 \ Å wavelengths, respectively, across the centers and peripheries of galaxies. To account for varying external radiation, we use a model of galaxy evolution and observe its impact on line brightness temperature. Our results indicate line brightness temperature varies by 0.5 K within the centers of galaxies and up to 1 K within the peripheries. Moreover, we find its impact on line brightness temperature to be similar to, although slightly less than, the effects of metallicity and star formation within the centers and peripheries, respectively. External radiation also modulates its intensity across the surfaces of galaxies, particularly in dwarf galaxies, where it may influence gas balance equations. Finally, since it is weaker than CO lines, the 15647 \ Å line of C I may be more sensitive to gas within the peripheries of galaxies.

Given an arrangement of $n$ lines in the plane and a set of points with their corresponding positions under the Hamming metric, we aim to determine the number of lines that intersect with the points, up to a shift in their positions. We establish that the number of lines required for unique representation, without any restriction on position shifts, is $\binom{n+2}{2}$, occurring when the lines form a convex polygon with $n$ sides. This result demonstrates that the arrangement must be a non-degenerate regular $n$-gon to guarantee distinct representations under the Hamming distance for any set of points.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by the gradual decline in orbital velocity of inspiralling compact binaries within the Milky Way. By employing an advanced signal model that leverages a range of accurate post-Newtonian terms, a team has demonstrated its value in improving the match filter response of PTA detectors, specifically for elliptical binaries containing neutron stars. Their analysis reveals that utilizing an optimized version of the signal model results in a 5-10 times improvement in the signal-to-noise ratio compared to an alternative standard model, depending on the frequency band in question. Furthermore, they have made the signal model publicly available through an online interface for generating match filter responses and predicting the characteristics of PTA targets, along with a comprehensive technical report detailing the methodology and implementation details of the model.

We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a second-class particle placed at the origin, will experience a velocity process that converges to -1 as time tends to infinity. Additionally, the spread of this particle will be compared to a root-mean-square that scales with time in a specific manner.

Our analysis compares and contrasts various mathematical models used to describe the dynamics of infectious disease spread, particularly in the context of the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic. By examining epidemiological parameters and different model-based predictions, we discuss their implications for public health policy. Although models have contributed significantly to our understanding of disease transmission and evaluation of control measures, their limitations also become apparent. These limitations stem from a narrow focus on mathematical representations, with insufficient consideration given to individual compliance and mass behavior, household transmission, community mobility, and infection prevention measures. As a result, our analysis suggests that models should be seen as tools for problem interpretation rather than problem definition. Furthermore, we advocate for an increase in research examining the complex interplay between individual and group dynamics, aggregation rules, and the consequences for pandemic outcomes.

We have theoretically analyzed multiple aspects of laser-induced three-body recombination in spinless and spin-polarized atom-dimer systems. When the collision energy matches a specific combination of the laser fields, we found that it leads to the destruction of a single spin-polarized atom and two dimers, resulting in the creation of two spin-polarized atoms. This process can be seen as a reverse of three-body recombination where three spin-polarized atoms are transformed into a single spin-polarized atom and a bound dimer. Our calculations also explored various outcomes of the process including the destruction of two spin-polarized atoms and a single dimer, or the creation of a spin-polarized atom and a Bose-Einstein condensate of two colliding components. We have further examined the process in spinless systems where it results in the destruction of two atoms and a single dimer, or the creation of a dimer from three colliding atoms. We have demonstrated that through proper selection of the laser frequency, both forward and reverse processes induced by colliding atoms and induced colliding dimers can be optimized for maximum output, and that the efficiency decreases exponentially with increasing collision energy.

Hierarchical data storage systems, particularly those with multiple levels of data, require efficient management to balance access speed and data expansion limitations. Our proposed method introduces a new storage structure that utilizes a binary tree hierarchy, allowing for optimized retrieval and updated data with minimal disruption to the existing dataset. Within this framework, we've developed an algorithm to determine the most beneficial node for insertion or deletion operations, ensuring maximum efficiency and a balanced tree structure. Our research also explores alternatives to our proposed structure, evaluating the performance of a linear hierarchy and a flat list storage system for comparative analysis.

Our proposed method utilizes the shallow water equations to model flood scenarios. In contrast to traditional approaches that rely on the Saint-Venant equations, our network can handle broken waves and overflow. Unlike conventional numerical methods, our solver leverages artificial neural networks to achieve speed-ups of a thousand times while maintaining accuracy comparable to established methods.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. We present a novel approach to HDR image creation, leveraging mobile devices' advanced processing capabilities. Our method, designed for mobile devices, employs a unique and efficient technique to select and blend photos at optimal exposure levels. Unlike existing methods that rely on complex, computationally expensive techniques, our approach is a straightforward, lightweight alternative utilizing a straightforward yet effective strategy to choose optimal exposure levels. Furthermore, we introduce a novel technique to fuse photos using weighted averages, which can be accomplished via simple arithmetic operations. Our approach, demonstrated through empirical testing, outperforms existing methods in terms of computational efficiency while producing HDR images on a par with those generated by more complex methods.

Causal neural networks are a relatively new concept that enables the disentanglement of causal relationships within complex data models. Without a standardized approach, researchers have employed varied methods such as graph-based models and time-series analysis. Our survey delves into the diverse uses and technical underpinnings of causal neural networks, covering models that detect directional connections, models that reconstruct historical data, and models that identify representative samples from complex datasets. We examine the theoretical foundations and technical implementation details of these models, concluding with the diverse range of applications in fields like social network analysis, genetics, and time-series analysis.

Given an infinite-dimensional manifold $N$, the Madsen-Weiss theorem demonstrates that the map $[ \text{what looks like } \Sigma^1_{g+1} ] \to [ \Sigma^1_g ]$ is surjective. To achieve this result, the authors prove that the Madsen-Weiss theorem implies the Madsen-Weiss b-formula, specifically in the instance where $2g-2 = 0$. By using the b-formula, they show that the Madsen-Weiss theorem is equivalent to the b-Mumford conjecture when $2g-2 = 0$. Furthermore, they demonstrate that the b-Mumford conjecture is viable for $2g-2 \geq 6$ by applying the b-ARF invariant. Alongside this, they provide an alternate proof of the 2-fold cover extension of the Madsen-Weiss theorem proved by the authors in [MW2].

the performance of their solvers and linear solvers, in particular. For cardiac
electro-mechanical models, the complexity is further amplified by the need to
solve multiple linear systems per time step. Due to the significant computational
cost of these systems, using a direct solver like LU is impractical for real-time
applications. In this work, the scalability of several linear solvers was evaluated
and compared, with the aim of identifying suitable options for implicit time stepping
in a clinical setting. A key finding is that the performance of solvers varies
markedly among different time steps and iterations, indicating that adaptive strategies
to switch between them could significantly enhance performance. Furthermore, a newly
introduced multilevel solver demonstrated promising results, outperforming other
solvers in multiple cases. A representative application with realistic heart rate variability
was utilized to assess the predicted solutions for accuracy and convergence.

Standard diffusion models are often challenged by the complex dynamics of various systems, including the diffusion of particles in turbulent environments and the spreading of biological substances within the human body. These scenarios exhibit unusual properties, deviating from the principles of standard diffusion. Specifically, the distribution of particle positions often displays strong asymmetry when analyzed over extended periods of time. To better understand these phenomena, a new model is proposed, incorporating the random distribution of a key physical property and is linked to a second model that ensures the probability distribution of particle positions remains asymmetric over time. The new model is then compared to existing alternatives, demonstrating its distinct features and differences.

Our research involves the development of a universal theoretical framework for analyzing optical resonators, micro-ring patterns, and waveguides with air claddings. We apply this framework to predict the spectral characteristics of these patterns in air claddings and investigate their linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions. We demonstrate how our approach enables the automatic generation of closed-form equations characterizing the spectral properties of complex pattern designs, including arrays and chiral structures. Furthermore, we derived a general nonlinear interaction equation that accounts for the beat length and phase mismatch in both linear and Kerr nonlinear regimes. Our findings are validated through comparisons with numerical simulations. We also examine a micro-ring array and demonstrate the predicted phenomena experimentally.

To better understand the complex dynamics of turbulent flows, particularly in enclosed systems, high-speed particle image velocimetry is a valuable tool. However, even with the advancement of PIV technology, there are limitations to its resolution, especially when it comes to high-frequency turbulent motions measured in a wide range of flow velocities. A novel approach has been proposed to enhance the resolution of turbulent flow dynamics through a generative adversarial network, enabling the prediction of high-frequency motion even at lower PIV resolution. A GAN-based model was created to enhance the resolution of multiple turbulent flow measurements at varying flow velocities, with a PIV resolution of 32x32 pixels, increasing it to a resolution of 1024x1024 pixels. The results showed that the GAN-based model accurately predicted high-frequency motion even at lower PIV resolution. A pre-trained model was also developed for the fast prediction of high-frequency motion, demonstrating its effectiveness in predicting dynamics in enclosed systems with varying flow velocities. A key finding of this research is that high-frequency turbulent motions in enclosed systems, even at moderate to high Reynolds numbers, can be characterized as highly irregular motion with little overall impact on the flow's energetic movement.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems. In response, the notion of considered reinforcement learning has emerged, accounting for past experiences when making future decisions. Although promising, the field's progress is hampered by the lack of accessible testing tools. To address this challenge, we present Lifelong Reinforcement Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge, open-source platform comprising 20 diverse, continuous testing scenarios. L2Explorer enables researchers to publicly evaluate lifelong reinforcement learning strategies and research on real-world problems. The system's underlying structure allows seamlessly integrating new tasks and scenarios, ensuring it remains highly versatile and accommodating. In a demonstration of L2Explorer's capabilities and the environment's own value, we incorporated a financially-related scenario and contributed a method called Memory-Efficient Progressive Curriculum (MEPC). Comparing MEPC to a standard approach across 5 diverse environments through the L2Explorer toolkit revealed notable performance gains, accompanied by substantial reductions in required memory.

A significant challenge in developing suitable methods for confident path navigation in large declarative process spaces is pinpointing the appropriate level of exploration versus re-direction. To address this issue, a new dynamic selection strategy known as CAVALRY is presented, leveraging a streaming approach to process representations. The method compares processes based on confidence levels, utilizing a scoring system that assesses process validity. Processes with lower scores are removed from consideration, streamlining the space to be explored. CAVALRY's design enables efficient and adaptive process filtering, as well as dynamic adjustment of the exploration versus re-direction balance by means of process score thresholds. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through comparative benchmarks against a leading alternative method.

This note provides an introduction to the interplay between geometric and algebraic approaches to compactifying moduli spaces. It starts by presenting the fundamental concepts and setting the context through basic examples and results. It then delves into more advanced topics, exploring connections between techniques from algebraic geometry related to geometric representations, specifically in the context of universal rationalities for algebraic groups. It also examines the algebraic aspects of compactifications of moduli spaces within the framework of schemes and algebraic geometry.

Determining the factors driving galaxy evolution through the combination of mass and star formation rate is crucial for understanding the role of environment, mass assembly, and active galactic nuclei in shaping galaxy development. The clear distinction observed in the mass-star formation rate plane, particularly evident for massive galaxies, suggests that factors such as bulge growth and active galactic nuclei feedback hold the key to interpreting the characteristics of massive galaxies in the present and past. By examining a comprehensive dataset that encompasses various observational techniques and extends to high masses and low star formation rates, we have derived and compared existing observational constraints on the mass of bulges and the mass of gas required to initiate star formation. For the majority of galaxies with moderate masses, we find that the mass of bulges and the mass of gas to form a HII region are in proportion, indicating that star-forming galaxies generally maintain a consistent relationship between their molecular gas and the mass of their disks. However, for massive galaxies with low star formation rates, we find that the mass of bulges outweighs the mass of gas by a factor of at least 5, indicating that the formation of massive bulges is driven by gas consumed through processes other than star formation within disks.

Determining sentiment in other languages is a significant challenge for machines translating text, especially when it comes to informal translations like those used on social media. To translate sentiment expressed through idiomatic phrases, machines need a vast amount of translated text including those phrases, which are often lacking in translated text available today. Our proposed approach addresses this issue by teaching machines to identify the sentiment in multiple languages simultaneously, thus enhancing their ability to translate the sentiment in each language. We demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach by pairing machines to translate the sentiment in English and one other language. The other language we used was Spanish, but our method can be applied to any other language. Our results showed that this approach leads to machines that can better translate the sentiment in the other language, even when they have little translation data.

X-ray images contain valuable clinical information that can be extracted and used for predictive purposes.  As such, we propose an innovative method for classifying COVID-19 patient ICU admission status based on image content, using a deep learning technique called Inception Score.  Specifically, we trained an Inception network on a dataset of image features representing x-ray images from patients with mild, moderate, or severe COVID-19 symptoms.  Our results show that the network's output can be used to distinguish between patients with severe symptoms, those with mild symptoms, or both categories.  We also found that Inception Score is correlated with ICU admission status, oxygen saturation levels, and lung infection severity in x-ray images.  By examining Inception Score components, we were able to identify key image characteristics associated with ICU admission, including the presence and location of opacities, their shape and whether they contain cavitation, the presence of bronchial dilation, and the amount of lung infection.  Our analysis suggests that Inception Score and Inception network architecture can be modified to enhance performance and accommodate data heterogeneity.

Given a global bundle E structured by means of an n-simplicial map, we establish an isomorphism between the global section group of E and the group of n-simplicial maps from a standard n-simplex to the base space B. This equivalence holds when the total space E is equipped with a coherent topology.

This paper delves into the issue of erroneous positives in visual relationship detection (VRD). It argues that the primary challenge lies in accurately categorizing relationships rather than detecting entities. To address this, it suggests modifying the standard double-attention mechanism used to combine entity and relationship features. The proposed network, called the Category-Aware Double Attention Network, incorporates a novel single-attention mechanism to combine entity and relationship features. It then uses a category-aware attention mechanism that assigns different weights to entity and relationship features based on their respective classification tasks. The paper also introduces a new category-aware fusion method that combines single-attention mechanisms in a way that adapts to the specific classification task. It demonstrates the efficacy of these proposed modifications through experimental results on the MS COCO-Kinship and Visual Relationship Detection datasets, showing that CADAN outperforms the current state-of-the-art models.

We're exploring the dynamics of galaxy evolution, particularly the development of their central bulges, using the lensing effect of a massive galaxy cluster from the early universe. By analyzing the distribution and movement of galaxies within the cluster, we're investigating how galaxies with disk shapes, once they've stopped accumulating matter, transform their mass and structure. The study focuses on the most massive galaxies in the cluster, examining their mass distribution, rotation patterns, and the composition of their stars. The research reveals that the central regions of these galaxies are unevenly shaped and feature prominent bulges that are formed through the merger of nearby galaxies. The study also finds that the formation of these galaxies slowed significantly about 2.5 billion years after the big bang, and the stars in the galaxies were formed over a relatively short period before that. The research suggests that the formation of galaxies like these was fueled by the consumption of gas and dust, the collision of nearby galaxies, and the influence of the cluster's gravitational field, leading to the creation of bulges and the evolution of their shapes over time. The study provides insights into the transformation of galaxies in the early universe, the role of interaction with the surrounding matter, and the relationship between star formation and the composition of the stars.

Recently discovered data from GCR monitors in Nov 2004 suggests that a significant increase in proton decomposition occurred during the solar event of Nov 7th, likely caused by a particularly powerful radiation burst in the form of a narrowband intense burst of neutrons. 

A model involving a sudden release of energy from the sun's surface, specifically solar neutrino burst analytics, provides insights into the characteristics of this event. 

Analysis of data from other monitors and solar observatories including SOHO, SDO, Geostationary Satellite Constellation, reveals the spatial distribution and duration of this event, as well as its impact on the Earth's magnetic field. 

A comparison with historical data from other solar events, particularly the Nov 13th event in 1971 and the Sept 1st event in 1989, highlights the distinct features of this nov 2004 event. 

A mathematical framework initially developed for electron decay dimensions is also applied to this event, along with implications for the Earth's atmosphere and biological effects due to high altitude jet stream interactions. 

A notable correlation with meteorological data and unusual weather patterns in Nov and Dec 2004 is observed. 

A possible link with the sudden disappearance of Arctic Sea Ice in 2007 is speculated, along with the potential for similar events in the past that may have contributed to global catastrophes like the massive flood of 471 CE in China.

During the ingestion of a massive planet by a young low-mass star with convective surface layers, the planet's angular momentum is transferred to the star, potentially causing its rotation rate to quicken. To assess the impact of this event on the star's rotation, we calculated its post-incorporation rotation rate for a wide array of scenarios. Our study reveals that even at the point of maximum angular momentum transfer, the star's rotation rate remains below its critical threshold for Li depletion and surface convection. Consequently, the star's surface rotation rate is expected to remain rapid for a limited duration, after which it returns to its pre-incident rate as the convective core shrinks. Our findings also indicate that the relationship between the initial eccentricity and the final rotation rate exhibits a distinctive pattern that varies with the mass ratio between the star and the planet. This pattern can be explained by the initial eccentricity's impact on the duration and extent of angular momentum transfer, which in turn is influenced by the planet's mass and the properties of the star's convective core.

The rapid dissemination of false news poses a significant threat to individuals,
society, and the world at large. The duration a false news story circulates
before being debunked is a key factor in determining its harmful consequences.
Social media platforms are struggling to accurately detect and remove false
information due to the dynamic nature of news. An emerging false news can
easily evade traditional fact-checking methods by leveraging fake or incomplete
information. In such cases, trust is often placed in the authority and expertise
of the publisher. Unfortunately, there is a growing number of untrustworthy
publishers emerging. As social media platforms continue to grow, the problem of
unreliable information is expected to intensify. To address this issue, a new
approach is proposed, focused on detecting false news that has recently emerged.
The suggested framework, ME-FEND, is a meta-model allowing for a start-up time
that is controllable and finite, is presented. ME-FEND extracts general information
from historical data and combines it with the current data to create a dynamic
neural network. Within a short time frame, false news that has recently appeared
can be identified based on diverse media sources. Experimental evaluations on two
datasets reveal that ME-FEND outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy.

We are considering the periodic conveyance equation, which is a variant of the Bachmann-Landau equation, to analyze its properties and examine the existence and smoothness of solutions within the framework of differential equations.

A recent study reveals that golay complementary sets can be constructed under specific binary matrix constraints using the permutation matrix structure, in turn derived from a specific block diagonal matrix design. These sets exhibit optimal binary sequence pair properties, ensuring maximum sequence pair distance and minimal weight under specific length constraints. Our research focuses on predictive models for sets with lengths that are not a multiple of four by exploring different parameter combinations in equation-based formulations. A key discovery involves linking pairs of sequence weight distributions to the exponential polynomial equations, thereby establishing conditions for valid set constructions. Additionally, our approach provides guaranteed output for sets with lengths that are near but not a multiple of four, offering opportunities for further advancements in this area.

Quantum spin orbit interaction in silicon enables coupling of electron spin with orbital motion through momentum matrix elements, giving rise to spin-orbit interaction and valley interaction which compete and valuably, complexly intersect. This important and distinctive feature results from silicon's diamond structured cleavage surface states and resulting directional and symmetrical (κ-shaped) electron energy contour, and thus accumulated electron distribution varies significantly across different Lattice Sites (LS) within the 2D atomic plane, potentially allowing for distinct in-plane spin and orbital control and manipulation through appropriate Lattice Site selection and local surface roughening. This unique functionality presents novel possibilities for robust execution protection against qubit decoherence, in addition to efficient execution of dual qubit operations like valley conditional transfer and valley-phason mediated spin transfer through appropriate interface engineering with neighboring atom planes.

Our investigation focuses on graph-based neural networks to analyze complex systems and their underlying dynamics. Through a meta-view of four specific applications (network analysis, disease transmission, financial markets, and human mobility) we demonstrate that a general framework combining network representation and neural network components can effectively capture fundamental dynamics. To further explore the relationship between network structure and dynamic behavior, we employed a strategy of fixed network topology and varied neural network parameters to extract essential features from the data. In examining the reconstructed components, we found that the original system's variables could be recovered through a transformation of the neural network's outputs, exposing a relationship between node representation and state transition. Ultimately, we discovered that across all examined cases, node representation and state transition are intertwined through a relationship defined by an affine transformation, whose components can be learned from data.

We investigate mappings that preserve the structure of a specific type of algebraic object called graded combinatorial modules. These modules can be constructed from elements called operators, using a process called geometric reinforcement, where mappings between them reflect the relationships between the operators themselves. Our goal is to count and describe these mappings in a way that connects them to the properties of another set of objects called cohomology operations. These operations take inputs from pairs consisting of spaces and classes, and produce outputs from the same type of class in different types of spaces. Our analysis also relates to a concept called Cartan complex, and its relation to mappings called Whitehead duals. Furthermore, we explore cases related to specific types of spaces called Steenrod modules, and provide a framework that can be used to extend our findings to similar scenarios.

A cutting-edge neuroimage is required for accurate prediction in neuroimaging diagnostics and treatments, but acquiring it involves significant time, effort, and expense. Artificial cerebral lesions have the potential to improve diagnostic accuracy and streamline clinical trials. However, generating highly realistic artificial lesions on a large scale is a significant challenge. To address this issue, an advanced neural network model called Progressive Adversarial Variational Auto-encoder was developed, capable of creating realistic artificial lesions across various brain regions. It consists of multiple variational auto-encoders organized in a hierarchical structure, which gradually refine the representation of cerebral lesions through encapsulation and adversarial training. When applied to real-world data, this model demonstrates significant improvements in generating realistic artificial lesions, with enhanced segmentation accuracy and a high degree of realism, as confirmed by clinical professionals. It can generate a vast number of artificial lesions across various brain regions, with a significant reduction in computational requirements.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification through reachability testing, which can be an imperfect but useful method due to its speed relative to other verification strategies. The GP 2 framework includes a runtime environment and a just-in-time compiler called GP 2-C, which leverages dynamic recompilation and various optimizations to enhance performance. GP 2-C operates by converting GP 2 programs into sequential form through graph transformations, followed by the application of control-flow and data-flow analyses to identify regions that contribute to program validation. A key aspect of GP 2-C is its capacity to handle programs containing side-effects, as well as its dynamic detection and blocking of infinite loops in the compiled code. Furthermore, GP 2-C includes a dynamic validation component that compares the compiled code with intended properties, incorporating features such as property checking, reachability testing, and bounds checking.

In recent years, due to the significant expansion of feature dimensions and the growing demands for more precise results, there has been an increasing interest in reducing data dimensions while maintaining or even improving accuracy. To achieve this, researchers have been exploring various techniques of feature extraction from a comparative learning framework, which compares the distinct characteristics of different classes and generates discriminative features for classification. Although such methods have shown superior performance in numerous scenarios, the underlying principles and connections between these methods remain not well understood. This paper aims to investigate the fundamental connections among these methods and provides a unified framework for feature extraction based on comparative learning, which includes both conventional and advanced techniques. Theoretical and experimental validations have confirmed the validity and effectiveness of this unified framework.

We have identified an infinite family of finite simple groups whose membership testing within the symmetric group's solvable quotient, when using the Knop-Shi theory, relies on verifiable equality of polynomial expressions involving Kronecker modules and symmetric functions. Notably, this polynomial equality can be generated using specific finite fields and polynomial operators, and it yields the finite group's explicit structure in the form of a twisted wreath product within the symmetric group.

Working with nominal data poses significant challenges, particularly when analyzing multivariate data. Variables in the data lack natural order, making it difficult to establish meaningful relationships and leading to sparsity methods being less effective. To overcome these obstacles, researchers have explored the use of group lasso and its variants by assigning a single parameter to each group of variables. However, this approach has a major drawback: it causes the groups to exhibit a form of'super sparsity' where only complete groups or nothing at all can be selected for analysis. To address this limitation, we developed an alternative method called the 'adaptive group lasso' or AGLO. AGLO assigns individual parameters to each variable within a group, enabling a mix of individual and group sparsity. In other words, it is possible to select individual variables from a group for analysis while excluding others. We implemented an efficient algorithm for the AGLO method and demonstrated its advantages through a series of numerical experiments and real-data examples.

Recent advances in large language models have shown the potential for a single model to be effective across diverse tasks, such as question-answering, text classification, and extracting information from narratives. To achieve this versatility, models are typically trained on massive generic text datasets that encompass a broad spectrum of topics and styles. In contrast, models trained on specialized data sources, like structured knowledge graphs, typically excel in more narrow domains but often struggle outside their trained scope. Our research involves examining the potential for a single model to be proficient in both general and specific domains without being tied to a particular training dataset. To demonstrate this capability, we developed a method for integrating structured knowledge into a large language model using a technique called knowledge structure learning. This technique enables the model to draw inferences from a vast amount of unstructured text, which is then converted into a structured format that can be combined with existing knowledge. When applied to well-established knowledge graphs like Wikidata, our approach enables the model to accurately identify relevant knowledge without being directly trained on the Wikidata dataset. When integrated with Wikidata, the model shows significant improvements over conventional approaches that rely on explicit linking between the text and knowledge graph.

High-resolution vector maps rely on the visual effectiveness of cartographic elements, particularly line junctions, which can be sources of distortion when rendered using current anti-aliasing techniques. Research on typography and graphics rendering overlooks the unique characteristics of line junctions, which differ significantly from curves, surfaces, and text. This study fills this gap by examining the visual impact of different anti-aliasing methods on line junctions within vector maps. It also explores alternative AA techniques and evaluates their performance through a crowd-sourcing study, revealing that a tailored approach called "CA" consistently ranks as the preferred method among participants. Further analysis of "CA" indicates that it excels at minimizing the distortion of line junctions, especially in the "7-segments" pattern, which is prone to severe degradation.

To enhance single-mixture speech separation, the siso network is a crucial component. We propose a dual-path convolution recurrent network (DPCRN) architecture for speech separation iso networks, which consists of two distinct pathways. The first pathway uses convolution recurrent modules to extract temporal features and a global sum to fuse the results for each channel. The second pathway employs convolution recurrent modules with channel-specific sum fusion and an attention mechanism to prioritize important time frames. We combine the two pathways, mixing their outputs with the target speech and rejecting the interference with complementary convolution filters. Models are trained to minimize the mean squared error between the clean and reconstructed signals. Our evaluation shows that the DPCRN model yields a 0.144 absolute improvement in STOI and 1.53 absolute improvement in SERR over the baseline iso network, demonstrating its effectiveness in speech separation iso networks.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models have shown significant improvement in simulated atmospheric convection when including moist air, making the approach highly promising for further development. Building on this progress, we have conceptually and numerically verified a two-fluid model by applying it to a simplified version of the Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection problem, which features buoyancy-driven turbulence driven by a temperature difference between the bottom and top plates of a closed chamber. The model includes a fluid less dense than the surrounding fluids and has been numerically implemented using the COSMOS-ART approach. By conducting a series of simulations with various temperature differences, we have validated the model's ability to replicate the characteristic convection patterns, the emergence of multiple roll structures, and the associated heat transfer patterns. Our results show that the model's performance compares favorably to the available theoretical predictions from the literature.

We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, labeling the systems 1 through 3. In these systems, we have two types of particles: mode A, which can be a bosonic mode or an atom or ion, and mode B, which must be a two-level system. We establish that even when the initial states of modes A and B across all systems are uncorrelated, we can create authentic entanglement between mode A in system 1 and mode B in system 3, along with mode A in system 2 and mode B in system 3, using specific dynamics including the interaction duration and strength. Our study also reveals that the success of this process relies on the systems being able to evolve for a half-integer number of their natural periods.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this paper, we examine the sentiment of Twitter posts in this context. To accomplish this,
we used a two-layer LSTM network, which we called SEFNet. This model includes an emotion
extraction layer and a classification layer. The emotion extraction layer is made up of two layers,
one for categorizing words into positive, negative, or neutral based on their parts of speech,
and another for determining the sentiment of each word by learning the overall sentiment
from the given tweet. The classification layer consists of two layers: one for sentiment
classification and another for sentiment confirmation. We gathered and manually annotated
a dataset of 15,000 English Twitter posts, known as TSE-Dataset. On this dataset, we tested
SEFNet and found that it outperformed six other techniques, including a single-layer LSTM.

In this work, we examine the connections between a nonlinear charged AdS black hole and a corresponding dual conformal field theory (CFT$_2$). Leveraging the AdS/CFT correspondence, we interpret the properties of the black hole as a response to various probe fields being introduced near its horizon. Through this analysis, we gain insights into the dual field theory's properties. Specifically, we show that the linearized responses of the black hole in question are identical to those of a linearized Reissner-Nordstr\"om AdS black hole within the context of linearized gravity. Furthermore, we determine the free energy and entropy of the dual field theory to be the same as those of the linearized Reissner-Nordstr\"om AdS black hole. Nevertheless, when the probe fields exert stress-energy that deviates from linear form, the properties of the dual field theory reveal itself through shadow measurements in its rest frame. By analyzing such shadows in the context of an infrared-regulated spacetime, we obtain the full free energy of the dual field theory, which is found to be in agreement with the total free energy of the black hole. Consequently, we can determine the logarithm of the entropy of the dual field theory as well as its irreducible part, along with an estimate of its action.

Our investigation focused on the effects of a qubit's state changes on its tomographic map. We studied how a controlled noise affects an arbitrary entangled state, specifically focusing on the impact on the map's structure and the degree of entanglement. Our results reveal that this noise initially disrupts the map's symmetry and eventually leads to a symmetrized version of the map as entanglement decreases. Furthermore, we observed the onset of map symmetry and increased entanglement in a Bell-diagonal scenario following a controlled noise disturbance.

360-degree virtual travel videos offer an immersive viewing experience but present challenges when it comes to navigation, due in part to the large amount of visual information they contain. To make navigation in these videos easier and more efficient, researchers have been exploring ways to predict the area of interest based on user captions. However, existing models primarily focus on determining the orientation of the video relative to the user, with limited consideration given to predicting the region within the video that the user will look at next. A new caption-based viewport forecasting model is presented here that utilizes a spatial attention mechanism and convolutional neural networks to accurately identify both the viewing direction and region of interest within the video. Evaluations using two distinct datasets demonstrate the model's superiority over existing methods in predicting the viewing direction and region of interest. Furthermore, the model's ability to forecast the region of interest is coupled with a steering signal derived from user input, enabling the model to demonstrate notable gains in region of interest prediction when compared to models without this signal.

Tensor network methods have effectively been utilized in researching discrete spin models and continuing field theories by approximating low-energy states and temporal evolution with minimal error. These models and theories typically feature complex interactions across nearby spins or field components. Research has shown that local, precise tensor networks can efficiently represent various models and theories by accurately capturing the dynamics of nearby spins or field components and incorporating leading order interaction details. These precise networks serve as optimal starting points for the development of various approximation methods. They can be made scalable by applying the variety of existing tensor network reduction methods in a way that maintains the accuracy of the approximation in the vacuum region. Far from the vacuum region, the accuracy of the approximation degrades in line with the complexity of the model or theory. It can be made even more efficient by applying the dust-yet-sharp approximation method. This research focuses on developing local, precise tensor networks specifically suitable for representing thermal states and the temporal evolution of spin and field systems. It also outlines possible approaches for obtaining such networks from available approximate ones. This is particularly relevant for research that uses the exact matrix product state approach to study one-dimensional spin models and field theories, as it provides a way to obtain precise local tensors from the approximate networks derived from those studies.

We introduce a decoupling framework "REDEC" that leverages restricted estimates to achieve a more refined understanding of how terms interact within an expression, thereby gaining insight into approximation methods. By analyzing a model scenario through the lens of redec, we uncover a relationship between the accuracy of a particular approximation and the characteristics of the terms being approximated. This relationship serves as a precursor to a more comprehensive result, namely that under certain conditions, a particular scale-oriented approximation results in the efficacy of a term being restricted, a concept that in turn facilitates a new estimate for a key expression within the Schrödinger equation. Ultimately, this new estimate yields a more compelling argument for a classical result, while also providing a framework for constructing explicit anti-convex barriers within the context of a related problem from harmonic analysis.

The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution, an important component of non-perturbative effects within small-x physics, is quantified by re-analyzing Balandin's calculation through a Chern-Simons functional method. In this study, the focus is on the 2-particle infrared renormalon within the gluon TMD PDF, and we determine the relevant non-perturbative parameter 'A' associated with this impact. Following this, the predicted characteristics of forward scattering, particularly the admissible range for rapidity extensions and the resulting estimates for neutron-proton scattering at small x, are compared to existing data and findings.

Research reveals that the intersection of magnetic and photonic fields leads to unique effects at the surface of metamaterials, resulting from spatial periodic structures, and this phenomenon is reflected in the optical properties. Until now, research has primarily focused on the basic principles and advanced applications, without differentiating the orientation of the optical field. In this study, we discovered a specific structure, comprised of gold nanorods and ferromagnetic stripes within a periodic lattice, where the optical properties are significantly impacted by the orientation of the electric field in relation to the magnetic field. When the incident light is perpendicular to the magnetic field, we observed an obvious redshift and enhancement of the splitting between the dipole and quadrupole resonance modes. In contrast, when the incident light is parallel to the magnetic field, the resonance modes showed little change. This unique orientation-sensitive magnetic field-dependent behavior could be utilized for controlling the optical properties with magnetic fields, specifically in sensing applications and the modulation of magnetophotonic effects.

Recent advancements in neural network reversals have been successful, particularly in securing stability and efficiency, as demonstrated by neutralized neural networks. These models, by removing the input influences, provide insights into how inputs are processed within the neural network. Despite their advantages, some applications, like black-box models based on decision functions, cannot utilize these models due to format incompatibility issues. To address this limitation, we propose a straightforward method for extracting crucial information from these models by inverse transformation. By means of this technique, we discovered the capability to transfer critical information to a new model without retraining, achieving notable performance enhancements. Our approach was particularly effective in handling significant changes, as seen in our experiments involving neural network updates.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±0.6) ×10^-4, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (2.8±1.0±0.3±0.2±0.4) ×10^-4, with the given uncertainties stemming from various sources.

We introduce an approach to construct the lattice of submodules of a multiplicity-free module that arises from the action of a Coxeter group on a complex irreducible representation. This approach involves examining the Bruhat order within the Weyl group of the Lie type underlying this complex irreducible representation. We provide a detailed analysis of how the lattice structure is affected by the choice of Lie type and its corresponding Weyl group. Furthermore, we demonstrate through examples and graphics the intricacies of these lattice structures.

Recent studies on learning from observations have shown improvements in safety
and efficiency for robotic systems by minimizing the need for human input.
However, the potential limitations of solely machine-learning-based methods
lie in the potential accumulation of errors, leading to suboptimal results.
To address this issue, a new framework, Co-Observation Learning, is proposed
to supplement systems with additional learning from a second observing system.
Without the necessity for expert guidance, this framework leverages the
second observation via a contrastive learning method, enabling the system to
combine observations efficiently while prioritizing data utilization over the
number of observing systems. Experimental evaluations on multiple scenarios
demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework in achieving accurate results
and reducing the number of observing systems required, as well as a comparison
with a baseline guided by human input.

This paper proposes a novel distance metric for Pulse-Audio-Coding (PAC) codes, which is necessary to determine the effectiveness of pulse coding protocols. By examining the relationship between the distance metric and packet error rates, the authors derive an accurate formula to calculate the minimum distance between PAC codes. This calculation involves the use of the Kiefer polynomial, which can be efficiently computed using the recursive formula derived in this study. Additionally, the authors introduce a set of rules to generate a comprehensive class of PAC codes with a known distance distribution. This knowledge can be leveraged to build high-performance pulse coding protocols.

Using reinforcement learning post optimization is highly effective for neural machine translation. Nonetheless, a challenge it poses is the extensive action space, which significantly hinders learning a suitable selection of actions. We propose a technique called dynamic action space reduction (DAR) that dynamically carves out the action space based on expected translation quality, thereby preventing suboptimal translations. We further investigate three different methods to determine the optimal set of actions and compare their efficacy. We demonstrate the superiority of our proposed dynamic action space reduction technique, achieving state-of-the-art results in several metrics including BLEU score, semantic similarity, and human evaluation.

Quantum systems that are connected to their surroundings through a dissipative interaction with multiple sources of noise are of great interest and exhibit rich dynamics. Under conditions of steady state, these systems driven by multiple sources of noise and allowing for back-action on the environment through their coupling, exhibit a variety of emerging phenomena. Here, we outline the experimental and theoretical treatment of a small, quantum system (qubit) driven by periodic light and in contact with two environments, represented by optical cavities on either side of the qubit. We show that, when the frequencies of the driving light and the cavities are close to one another, the steady state state becomes a periodic structure in the Fourier domain, supported by both theoretical modeling and actual measurement of the output fields from the cavities. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this periodic structure holds important value for landmark frequency ratios as evidence.
We explore how several key operator repetitions on biharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean space lead to key properties of these hypersurfaces.

A real number space $X$ is called harmonic if every non-degenerate interval contains the harmonic mean of its endpoints. Harmonic spaces are closely related to electric networks and have been extensively studied, incorporating results from various fields including geometry, analysis, and graph theory. The main focus of this study is the connection between recognizable sets in the rational space and harmonic spaces. A set in the rational space is identified as recognizable if it can be distinguished by a function that is based on harmonic means within given intervals. The paper explores several characteristics of recognizable sets, including their structure, behavior under transformations, and relationship to convex spaces.

MongoDB, a leading NoSQL database, has gained widespread acceptance due to its flexibility, scalability, and efficiency. To ensure data consistency across NoSQL databases like MongoDB, a well-established theory based on constraint checking is utilized. However, validating the consistency of NoSQL databases through transactional integrity has not been well studied and requires a different approach. In the course of investigating MongoDB's consistency, we discovered its complex documentation and lack of clear guidelines on consistency levels of database operations. Furthermore, we found that operation consistency is determined by consistency levels, which in turn are influenced by multiple factors including operation type, transactional behavior, and background operations like paging and eviction. To demonstrate the applicability of our approach to real-world scenarios, we developed a method to specify and validate transactional integrity using UAutomizer/UPA, and using this method we validated the transactional integrity of MongoDB with its default storage engine and Extended JSON document model.

Using the elementary symmetric polynomial basis, we demonstrate the $e$-positivity of chromatic symmetric polynomials from both the Bjorner-Welsh and the Stanley conjectures. Additionally, we provide a formula for the coefficients of these polynomials and show that the inverse Kostka matrix contains significant information about these coefficients. As a result, we find that the entries of the inverse Kostka matrix are nonnegative for the smallest nontrivial cases.

Our investigation delves into the intricate dynamics and concealed geometry of a specific type of complex network, namely a triangular-kagome isomer, which comprises individual non-covalent interactions between molecular components. By interposing these interactions with energy barriers and converting them into a potential landscape, we obtained a clearer understanding of the assembly's geometry and how it influences the dynamics of spin reversal through metastable states and potential barriers. Our findings reveal that a specific scaling of the geometric disorder can lead to a characterization of dynamic state in terms of disorder type, thereby identifying distinct dynamical states in the assembly's parameter space. We demonstrated that the introduction of imperfections in the triangular-kagome geometry disrupt the large-time entropy and slow dynamics, the hallmark of a specific state that maps onto a rational geometry only after accounting for the introduced defects.

We analyzed 32 nearly identical orbits of the fast solar wind within 0.25 AU from the sun using data from the Quakes experiment on board the Parker Solar Probe. The observations were made at a frequency of 1 Hz with a 50 ms time resolution, allowing the calculation of energy spectra for individual samples of the solar breeze energy flow. These spectra revealed an almost universal power law energy distribution, consistent with theoretical predictions from 2010. The observed energy distribution had a peak frequency of approximately 1.8 Hz and was independent of solar breeze velocity, density, or total solar breeze energy density. The energy of the largest turbulence is likely to be compared with the kinetic energy of the solar breeze, which is influenced by the inner heliosphere's solar wind conditions and can vary significantly within a distance of 1 AU from the sun.

To enhance speech interaction efficiency, incorporating emotion recognition into speech command systems is vital. Despite advances in speech emotion recognition, it remains a challenge to apply it in practical command systems due to limited training data and performance variability across domains. We address these issues by developing a domain-agile DRL-based architecture for speech emotion recognition in a multi-class setting. The proposed method leverages two learning processes: initial knowledge acquisition through a general model and targeted adaptation within a specific domain. We evaluate this architecture using two separate datasets for both training and testing and find it significantly outperforms a baseline model. Moreover, it levers state-of-the-art performance when compared to other domain adaptation methods using either a single dataset. We also test the practical applicability of this architecture by integrating it into a DRL-based system for speech interaction and measure its performance using both emotion recognition and interaction accuracy as evaluation criteria.

Researchers explored the development of intense shocks in a uniformly expanding cosmos with a spherical void, using a new approach that combines the thin-shells model and the self-similar method. They discovered that in a model representing an expanding cosmos with a growing void, there is a critical point where the shock waves become unstable, demonstrating through perturbation analysis and numerical integration. Additionally, they found that in a model representing an expanding cosmos with a constant size void, the edge of the void is surrounded by a layer where the matter density increases infinitely quickly, thus validating an earlier result obtained using an approximate method.

Using $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ data, a study in QCD approaches evaluated the impact of nonperturbative effects within $B$ mesons. Specifically, contributions were assessed for gluon field averages beyond the scope of vacuum saturation and the distribution of $D_s^{-}$ mesons within $B_s^0$ systems. The research focused on multiple factors including $d/q$ ratios, $D_s^{-}$ momentum distributions, and $B_s^0$ decay length spectra. The study employed LCDM2, CLEO-III, and D0 data sets, with outcomes expressed in terms of color electric field strength and $B_s^0$ lifetime components.

Building on the connection established in [13, Chapter 7], we demonstrate in this study that generalized Hermite polynomials are linked to monodromy-free Schrödinger operators with rational coefficients through their construction. This relationship enables us to derive an explicit formula for the constructed polynomials, which can be viewed as an extension of the classical Gaussian hypergeometric formula. Furthermore, this connection results in an infinite set of orthogonal polynomials when we set a specific parameter to 1. As a significant application, we produce eigenfunctions for the one-dimensional Landau-Lifshitz gyroelectric spin chain using our constructed polynomials, given the chain's Hamiltonian is related to the Schrödinger operator with a parameter set to 1.

The consistent pattern of noise generated through stick-slip motion in an adhesive tape system holds significant value for further study and potential application in several fields. The dynamic process that the tape undergo through to produce sound was examined using high-speed cameras, along with a sensor for measuring force and audio recording equipment. The results indicate that the noise produced through the process does not follow a random pattern, but rather a more structured and predictable model that includes periods of significantly reduced audio levels, referred to as 'quiet phases.' These quiet phases were discovered to occur when the tape undergoes a specific unwinding movement, known as the 'peel arrest phase.' By preventing this peeling movement, the noise and quiet phases can be significantly reduced to a near-silent state.

We illustrate the significance of non-abelian Wess-Zumino terms in Chern-Simons gravity, which leads to the identification of non-abelian topological charges and their associated conservation laws. These laws emerge from the non-abelian version of the ether theorem and find non-trivial expressions in vacuum states with non-trivial topological characteristics, such as the state of a black hole or a cosmological space-time with a constant curvature. Furthermore, these charge conservation laws are reflected in specific observables in gravity, which become invariant in these states of vacuum. We then examine the breaking of these states through perturbations and the resulting oscillations in the gravitational field, which provide insights into the relationship between the ether theorem and linearized gravity. We also consider the quantum framework, where we demonstrate that these non-abelian Wess-Zumino terms lead to non-trivial topological charge conservation laws in the quantum theory, which are reflected in specific observables in gravity, resulting in an invariance principle similar to that in the classical context.

To prevent counterparty risk resulting from option hedging, a margin or collateral is required to cover potential losses due to the option holder's default. The size of this requirement, also known as the credit value of an option (CVO), depends on the option's characteristics, the counterparty's credit risk, and the risk-free rate. When accounting for expenses related to hedging costs and credit, the CVO becomes more complex, especially under stochastic interest rates. In the absence of closed-form solutions, finite difference methods can approximate the option's collateral value, but these methods are typically computationally expensive and less practical for real-time usage. Here, we derive an analytical formula to estimate the option's collateral value under the presence of hedging expenses, credit risk, and stochastic interest rates, enabling the efficient management of counterparty risk.

A higher education system serves as the basis for a dynamic model where opportunities are shared across generations. The analysis focuses on how institutions are ranked to provide opportunities and how these rankings affect the chance that a family will gain better opportunities for their child. The key findings are as follows: if some families have access to better institutions, the opportunities they gain will, in turn, benefit the children of other families; however, this boost in opportunities is only temporary and eventually disappears; and the chance that a family will gain better opportunities for their child is determined by whether the available institutions to them are better than those available to their child. The implications of these findings are examined within the context of a changing environment, social mobility policies, and across different types of families.

A method called "brightness scans" is proposed to determine the characteristics of an electron beam by measuring the intensity of an emitted signal across a screen that spans a wide angle. Bivariate Gaussian models can be used to represent both the beam distribution and the signal pattern, allowing us to calculate the signal characteristics through beam distribution parameters and signal pattern properties. The proposed method is particularly useful for analyzing high-brightness beams in environments where detailed knowledge of the beam characteristics is crucial, such as in HOM (higher-order mode) beam monitors at third-generation storage rings.

This paper presents a distributed optimization framework for minimizing a function whose structure is revealed to individual agents, utilizing gradient descent with security constraints. The study demonstrates the convergence rate of this approach is directly proportional to the square of the maximum deviation of agents' true parameters. A quantized gradient descent algorithm is then introduced and proven to converge at a rate directly related to the square of the maximum deviation of the quantization intervals. The study further shows that a robust gradient descent algorithm can reduce the impact of malicious agents on system performance. The results are illustrated through simulation experiments.

The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness is overwhelmed by instrumental limitations and foreground contamination, necessitating sophisticated analysis techniques. Effective interpretation of future data from more sensitive experiments, with better angular resolution and advanced detector arrays, requires a precise assessment of instrumental influences on the data, particularly since such effects will increasingly dominate the measurements.
