We examine the formation of nuclear star clusters at the hearts of massive galaxies and identify how factors such as mass, rate of star formation, and mass of the central black hole influence the merger rate of compact binaries originating from these clusters. Using an advanced model of galaxy evolution and observing these clusters through the lens of a nearby galaxy, we estimate the gravitational waves produced by binary mergers within these clusters over the course of thirteen billion years of cosmic history. Our predictions for merger rates vary widely, from as low as $1.5 \times 10^{-5}$ to $69.7$ per year, depending on parameters such as the mass of the cluster, rate of star formation in the galaxy, and mass of the central black hole. This range is reflected in our models of the gravitational wave spectrum, which spans an incredible five orders of magnitude.

A new method is proposed to enhance the physical layer security of wireless communication systems that use dual-hop AF relaying technology and multiple-input multiple-output technology. The proposed method involves optimizing multiple parameters including the power allocation to subcarriers and the input signals to the relay and destination. By utilizing majorization conjugate duality, the originally hard non-convex problem is converted into an iteratively solvable and convex problem. Through simulation results, the proposed method is shown to enhance the end-to-end rate and the rate gap at low SNR ranges, and to find the optimal tradeoff between security and data transfer rate.

Text-based games serve as an effective platform for evaluating goal-oriented language models by testing their ability to navigate, absorb information, and make informed decisions through text interactions. The rapid progression in text-based models can be attributed to the development of advanced training methods like reinforcement learning with actor-critic algorithms and the creation of large language models. To cater to the increasing scale of models, the TextWorldExpress platform has been designed to support the rapid playback of text-based games at incredibly high speeds, one million steps per second, without the need for retraining the underlying model. This acceleration technique leverages a simple yet efficient method of playback, combining a limited history of previous actions, observations, rewards, and done flags to enable quick determination of the model's next action. The TextWorldExpress platform has been applied to nine diverse text-based games, resulting in models that can be trained to a level of one million steps in approximately one day on a single GPU.

Deep learning models, in particular LSTMs, have been successfully applied to various time series recognition tasks, including video identification. However, these models require large amounts of computational resources and generate significant amounts of waste heat in practice. To address this issue, a novel method is proposed to optimize LSTM networks based on Tucker tensor decomposition and Monte-Carlo block fusion. The model's architecture was designed in parallel with its implementation using a 0.13um CMOS technology. The results show that the model's memory can be reduced to 23% of its original size while maintaining the same accuracy, and the energy consumption during inference can be decreased by 88x. A custom hardware implementation is compared to a virtual software implementation using PyTorch, demonstrating the benefits of co-design.

In a theory with a well-defined stress-energy tensor within a CFT framework, the energy-momentum tensor of any operator is directly related to its two-point function. This relationship leads to the expectation that the energy-momentum tensor of a BPS operator in a d=4 SCFT will have a non-negative definite 4x4 stress-energy tensor symmetry matrix component. We have observed this expected behavior in a multitude of examples, spanning across various types of operators including chiral ring members, SYM coupled to certain types of vector and scalar fields, as well as certain BPS operators within the 3d and 5d SCFT spectra. Building upon these observations, we have formulated two conjectures regarding the positive definiteness of specific 4x4 matrices. When examining the energy-momentum tensor of a single operator within a 4d SCFT setup, we found that only one of the two matrices in question is always positively definite. In contrast, when considering the energy-momentum tensors of pairs of operators in 4d SCFT, we found that the combination of their sum is positively definite in all cases studied. This finding is in line with the expected outcome based on general principles of the AdS/BCFT framework. Moreover, we have also established the expected relationship in 3d and 5d SCFT settings.

Given an integral domain (K, v) with a discrete valuation v and a non-trivial v-module Q, we establish criteria for the tight Hilbert polynomial to be well-defined within this context. It is necessary and sufficient that a specific set of conditions, which includes the property of being able to distinguish polynomials based on their degrees, is met. Additionally, when (K, v) contains a field of uncountable size, these conditions are equivalent to another set of requirements, specifically that a particular invariant called F is finite and distinct for distinct degree values.

Recently, the rise of platform economies and the growth of the gig work sector have highlighted the need to review traditional employment models and the policies surrounding them.  As a result, there is growing interest in researching the dynamics of platforms, workers, and consumers through the lens of labor market policies.  This paper focuses on a specific procurement model, the supplementary services procurement model, which it uses as a micro-level laboratory to examine the effects of policy interventions in the gig economy.  It also presents a cooperative game theory approach to analyzing the model's equilibria and the impact of policy changes on consumers, workers, and platforms.  Furthermore, it conducts an empirical analysis using data from China's gig economy and finds that labor platforms' market power has a negative effect on workers' earnings, while government subsidies and regulations exert distinct influences on platforms' profits and workers' earnings.  It also explores the empirical consequences of policy changes on consumers, workers, and platforms.  It is hoped that this research's theoretical and empirical results can provide policy makers with insights into forming effective labor market policies in the gig economy.

Given a polynomial $P(x)$ and a real number $c$, we examine the sequence defined by $P_n(x) = P(P_{n-1}(x))$ with its roots, especially those that map to $c$ under an inverse transformation, denoted as $r_{n,k}(x)$. The structure of these roots is revealed by decomposing $P(x)$ into its prime factors and analyzing the composition of the corresponding quadratic components. This analysis exposes a pattern in the roots of $P_n(x)$, which can be extrapolated to a broader, more abstract context involving a product of quadratic factors rather than a composition of primes.

Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm vortices. During its approach to summer, a rare hexagonal cloud feature has been observed surrounding the developing polar vortex in Saturn's northern hemisphere. The formation of this vortex is similar to that found in Earth's polar atmosphere, indicating that Saturn's had a similar phenomenon in its past. The formation of the hexagonal cloud pattern was accompanied by changes in atmospheric circulation patterns, including the formation of polar clouds, wind shifts, and temperature fluctuations. The appearance of the hexagon was first noted in 2018, but it has since faded from view.

This paper investigates solutions to the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation within a convex boundary, particularly in a spherical domain. When energy solutions are considered, we find that beyond a certain critical point, solutions expediting energy growth are inevitable. Additionally, in a Euclidean setting, solutions on an infinite domain that exhibit energy growth are also shown to be unavoidable. These results build upon the foundational work of Glassey, Holmer, and Nakanishi, and the approach employed relies on a recent energy estimate by Doderich, Gubin, Holmer, and Nakanishi.
We establish the existence and distinctiveness of local characterizations for algebraic varieties within the context of a specific abstract setting that includes the ambient context.

We establish that for any graded collection of vector spaces with a distinguished component and a given nilpotent endomorphism, there is a well-defined concept of polarization. This concept is then demonstrated to be closely related to the polarization of a single vector space equipped with a scalar product, specifically through the use of a particular scalar product when the dimension of the space is even. Furthermore, we identify specific conditions under which the polarization of a single space can be extended to the collections, including the scenario where the underlying field has a characteristic of two.

Given a locally compact group G and a compact subset omega of G, this work establishes the equivalence of two expressions that calculate the relationship between orbital integrals and the adjusted measure on omega. These expressions, which take the form of an operator that calculates the relationship between an integral over orbits within G/K by means of the right translation by a element within omega and the adjusted measure on omega, for a fixed maximal compact subgroup K of G, are shown to be equal through a series of computations. Alternatively, this equality can be derived from a more general result that compares the operator to an average of the right translation by a single element within omega and is valid for any measure on omega.

The success of stage retrieval in nuclear physics is closely tied to the accuracy of density profiles obtained from spectroscopic analysis, particularly in the context of heavy heavy-ion collisions where high energy densities may lead to quark gluon plasma formation. A key challenge arises from the complex and often model-dependent relationship between spectroscopic signals and density profiles, compounded by limited access to high resolution density profiles. A novel approach is proposed to address this challenge by leveraging x-ray resonance scattering cross sections, which exhibit a notable enhancement in the forward hemisphere and in the outer regions of the collision system, making them remarkably sensitive to the surface layer of the collision fireball. As such, this signal exhibits unique characteristics that distinguish it from other x-ray signals, offering a straightforward path to isolating its contribution and enhancing the accuracy of stage retrieval analyses, especially in heavy ion collisions where the surface layer may hold significant influence over the evolution of the collision system.

A novel method is being presented to model single-phase Darcy flow within fractured porous media, utilizing a unique mixed finite element approach. This technique involves two distinct elements: conforming polygons for the main medium and a specific type of mini-element for the fractures, which are one-dimensional spaces within the framework of $C^0$ continuity. A range of mini-element techniques is being introduced for the first time, which can be applied to fracture elements while ensuring the balance equation remains solvable and the pressure gradient along the fractures is smooth. A hybrid discontinuous Galerkin approach is being employed to discretize and solve the flow equations within both the fractures and the main medium, with consistent results showing this method offers a cost-effective alternative to the standard hybrid mixed finite element technique.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis in practice is often hindered by the significant computational resources required for this purpose, particularly when utilizing advanced approximation methods like Bayesian model averaging and expectation maximization. This paper addresses these challenges by presenting an optimized workflow utilizing the PyBF platform to streamline Bayes factor analysis in Python, along with a comprehensive overview of the scientific methodology underlying this process. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method by applying it to a sample dataset from the cognitive science literature, and make the PyBF platform, including the workflow presented here, openly and freely available to the scientific community.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an already established semantic connection. Such a model can be utilized for interpreting the predicted relationships between sentences. It can also be employed for the automated analysis of discourse indicators in constructed text samples. This paper presents a trained model and an automated analysis tool called DiscSense which enables users to input a set of sentences and automatically analyze the predicted relationships between their semantic connections, identified corresponding discourse indicators, and the implied semantics.

We investigate the structure of a specific family of functions associated with the optimization of a positive definite matrix within the cone of completely positive semidefinite matrices, specifically those with fixed rank. Through the introduction of an appropriate isometry, we analyze the layout associated with this family of functions, discovering its invariants. The layout invariants are characterized as the intersection of several quadratic surfaces, each representing the projection of a sphere of varying radius within a higher-dimensional space. The number and configuration of these surfaces' intersections are determined by the rank of the matrix at hand. Consequently, we demonstrate that functions within this family exhibit varying levels of convexity, including both local and global convexity, with the degree of convexity dependent on the specific rank of the matrix.

A recent paper proved that any cubic bipartite graph could be colored using three colors in a way that no adjacent edges are tinted with the same color, and did so by an iterative process known as edge-tinting. This achievement has been seen as a significant advancement, as it implies all bipartite graphs that can be obtained from cubic bipartite graphs by a sequence of edge-contractions are three-tuple free. However, our research presents a counterexample to this claim of superiority over a different condition known as three-tuple freedom.

We employed coevolutionary genetic programming to observe the emergence of a Nash Equilibrium in symmetric Cournot games. Our research revealed that the stability of NE relies on a balance between two key factors: the level of noise present and the degree of population interconnection. When noise is significant or connections are limited, a state approaching NE can arise even if the initial state is random. However, with minimal noise and extensive connections, the population may become trapped in a nearby optimal state rather than converging to NE.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $D$, with vertices $V$ and edges $E$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and normal power functions behave in a similar manner for edge ideals associated with $D$. Concretely, we find that the $e$th symbolic power of an edge ideal linked to $D$ contains the $f$th normal power of this ideal if and only if $e$ surpasses a specific integer $g$, which is dependent on $D$ and includes the function $f$ as a factor. Additionally, we provide lower and upper bounds for the minimal integer $g$ mentioned above.

Convolutional neural networks are vulnerable to various forms of noise that can significantly affect their performance. To overcome this, researchers have been exploring ways to make these networks more resilient to noise. Our study examines the potential of activation interval supervision as a means of enhancing the noise-resilient capabilities of convolutional neural networks. To validate this potential, we constructed a training method that incorporates activation interval supervision and tested it on models trained to distinguish between authentic and manipulated images. The results showed that this method improved the noise-resilient capabilities of these models in multiple scenarios. Furthermore, we discovered that incorporating activation interval supervision as a regularizer in a traditional training framework can lead to models that are more resistant to noise that occurs during measurements, specifically under qubit-based binary neural network measurements.

We introduce a new type of Jordanian twist, which is a part of Jordanian twists that have been extensively studied. We provide a one-parameter group of this twist and offer explanations for its properties. Furthermore, we include an expression for its associated 2-cocycle and demonstrate that it meets specific requirements by mapping it to the appropriate double cross product algebra.

We propose a novel framework that simultaneously builds a shared semantic space across languages and reduces linguistic diversity within each language. This framework leverages clustering techniques to achieve both inter- and intra-lingual semantic alignment. By organizing words into clusters based on their representation, we use the latent cluster structure to refine word representations in each language, resulting in a more unified semantic space across languages and reduced disambiguation within each language. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by conducting multilingual classification and we compare it to other methods of word clustering and semantic alignment.

The paper presents first-data from the LHC for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV, comparing pion, kaon, and proton production with 8.16 TeV Pb-Pb collisions and evaluating the nucleus-nucleus collision density via φ-meson production.

Starting in October 2019, violent protests and unprecedented social unrest gripped Chile, with riots and looting reported in over 80% of the country's municipalities. Our analysis aims to examine demographic variables that contributed to the likelihood of protests occurring in each region, using a non-local SIR model as a secondary area of exploration. By incorporating both local and external factors that influenced infection spread, we adapted the model to also incorporate variables that contributed to protest escalation in each municipality, using a comprehensive dataset compiled by the Chilean National Statistics Institute. In the model, we replaced the constant infection rate with a more dynamic variable, correlating it to demographic characteristics and distance from Santiago, the country's capital. Our analysis of the data revealed factors that increased the risk of protests occurring in each municipality, including a higher percentage of young people, lower average income, greater dissatisfaction with governance, and higher distances from Santiago. We found that once activated, protests tended to spread from surrounding municipalities at a speed of approximately 32 kilometers over the course of two days, with our model predicting that riots and looting would break out in over 80% of the country's municipalities in line with real-world events.

This research develops an innovative technique for addressing the emptiness problem in the context of regular expressions with additional operators, specifically the ability to repeat patterns using integers or according to a specified pattern, the ability to choose between alternatives, and the ability to ignore certain input. We demonstrate the applicability of this technique to various scenarios, including the verification of finite-state automata, validation of regular expression constraints, and validation of XML or regular expression-based data constraints.

Mobile agents require a position estimate to navigate safely and efficiently.
They often collaborate with models, using sensor data from inertial sensors and
images, and learning from deep neural networks through end-to-end training.
However, inertial sensors and the learned models they work with have limited
memory, making it difficult to apply complex models. In response, we developed
the External Memory Attention Visual-inertial Odometry, or EMA-VIO, algorithm,
using external memory to facilitate efficient navigation. The EMA-VIO model
incorporates both current and historical data in its calculations, using an
attention-based mechanism to process it. We tested the EMA-VIO algorithm on
publicly available datasets, comparing it to other navigation algorithms.

Our investigation delves into the characteristics of Weyl semimetallic behavior under the influence of elevated order interactions. Using $K$-space coupling and drive-damping approaches within a 3D tight-binding model, we demonstrate that certain interactions, such as higher-order terms and DMI, are capable of elevating the order of Weys semimetallic behavior while maintaining stability in the spectrum and Weyl point locations. However, we find that strong drive or damping can either move Weyl points to the edge of the Brillouin zone, result in their merging, or lead to a transition to another semimetallic state. Furthermore, we observe that driven or damped perturbations can induce an anisotropic anisotropy in the energy spectrum, leading to the emergence of square-root singularities in specific directions within the BZ.

This study presents a numerical approach to resolving a data completion problem for the Maxwell equations, focusing on the recovery of missing data within access restricted areas. A weak formulation of the inverse problem is established and a quasi-reversibility approach serves as the numerical framework. Key aspects, such as stability, convergence, and accuracy of the method are demonstrated through theoretical proof. Moreover, results from numerical experiments are presented, showcasing the method's effectiveness in recovering data within obstructed areas and highlighting its sensitivity to various constraints, including the impact of mesh refinement, timetomainframe, and electric conductivity variations.

The surge in distributed knowledge bases has brought forward a significant challenge in integrating them, as the process is often manual, time-consuming, and subject to individual judgments. This research addresses the problem of selective integration in distributed knowledge bases by constructing an optimized result through federation. We call this process Federated Selective Integration (FSI). Unlike traditional approaches that aim to combine all available information, FSI leverages algorithms to identify optimal data sources and information for integration. We develop a framework for FSI that incorporates multiple optimization objectives and strategies for achieving balance between precision and efficiency. Moreover, we extract key factors that affect the performance of FSI and analyze them using our developed framework. We also introduce performance predicates as a key concept to enhance the efficiency of FSI. Finally, we apply our framework to a knowledge fusion task and present its benefits in terms of performance improvement.

We analyze the rank of elliptic curves from quartic extensions in the rational numbers, focusing on those under the Galois group $S_4$ and a specific subgroup of index 4 within it, $\Delta_{4} \simeq A_4 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$. For $S_4$, we show that the rank of an elliptic curve in a quartic extension over the rationals is not bounded as the prime contributes to the Kronecker limit formula has an infinite number of contributions from the four Galois orbits of 2-torsion points. Furthermore, under the assumption that the Chebotarev-Kim rank conjecture holds for all primes with squarefree conductors, we find a lower bound for the rank of elliptic curves in quartic extensions under $S_4$ as $\frac{1}{4} \prod_{p \in S_4} \left( 1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{p}} \right)_{\text{ramify}} \left( 1 - \frac{2}{\sqrt{p}} \right)_{\text{inert}} \cdot \left( 1 - \frac{4}{\sqrt{p}} \right)_{\text{inert}} \cdot \left( 1 - \frac{9}{\sqrt{p}} \right)_{\text{inert}} \cdot \left

A crucial boundary, the quantum focussing boundary, exists within the complex terrain of spacetime geometries that bounds the development of singularities. Studies focusing on the quasi-local quantum gravity scenario through holographic principles have identified this boundary as the locus where the surface gravity becomes negative, leading to an exponential decline in the width of the entanglement region. Through an exploration of holographic theories in both asymptotically aditive and non-aditive spacetimes, we demonstrate the validity of this condition by computing the surface gravity via both local and quasi-local methods. Consequently, we derive constraints on the change in the width of entanglement, which is found to be directly related to the change in the area of the entanglement region. Furthermore, we provide a simplified expression for the change in area in terms of the change in the width of entanglement, which is then applied to an example involving a holographic disk system undergoing a quadratic expansion.

Quantum systems, described by their dynamic trajectories within a Hilbert space, evolve according to complex patterns that are sensitive to changes in their parameters over time. To understand these evolution patterns, we must establish the uniqueness of their parameterization. This condition, known as identifiability, is critical for reversing the dynamics to recover the system's initial state. In this research, we examine the identifiability of a two-level system's dynamics on its Bloch sphere by analyzing the uniqueness of its trajectory for both continuous and discrete time models. For a broad range of Markov processes, including Lindblad dissipative dynamics, we define a key asymmetry measure to determine the shape of the identifiable region in the parameter space. As a specific example, we investigate the identifiability of a damped harmonic oscillator and find that its coherent amplitude becomes identifiable within three times the system's natural period, whereas its damping coefficient takes significantly longer to identify. Furthermore, we derive a lower bound on the time required to identify the asymmetry of its trajectory, which provides a quantum speed limit. In addition, we explore the effects of discrete time models on the system's identifiability and find that they result in more complex, non-monotonic identifiable regions.

We develop a theory of continuous operators that act on functions within the Lebesgue space $L^p(\Omega)$, where $\Omega$ represents a domain within $\mathbb{R}^n$. These continuous operators must satisfy a significant property: they map bounded functions to functions with a well-defined bound within the space $L^p(\Omega)$. We establish a key estimate that enables the comparison of the norm of an operator within the space $L^p(\Omega)$ to the value of an auxiliary function, which serves as a norm-like quantity. We derive several important consequences from this estimate, including the equivalence of the norm of an operator to the supremum of the absolute value of an expression that contains its characteristic and the Lebesgue measure of the domain $\Omega$. We also demonstrate the possibility of exchanging the role of the norm with the supremum, which is a crucial feature with far-reaching implications.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. Our study focuses on analyzing a popular microwave resonator design that uses diamond-shaped elements made of silicon. We utilized a Calabrese-Letta T-2 time measurement method to determine the effects of defects on T-2 times and identified areas with high T-2 times through 3D spatial mapping. The analysis revealed that T-2 times are influenced by the local electric field and vary in response to changes in geometry. Furthermore, we discovered that T-2 times are associated with the formation of standing waves within the resonator.

Our research delves into the atmosphere's evolution from its initial state on Mars-sized Venus to its present condition, considering impacts from the planet's solidification, solar energy, and the retention of water. By analyzing various factors and their interconnections, we uncover key processes and feedback loops that have shaped the atmosphere over time. The study reveals that the current atmosphere of Venus can be explained by a combination of its initial conditions, Earth-Venus differentiation processes, and the significant retention of water in the form of hydrogen retained in minerals and chemical bonds with silica, thereby preventing a runaway greenhouse effect.

Point processes are used to model the occurrence times of events in various fields, including finance, neuroscience, and genetics. A key aspect of these processes is the influence of past events on the rates of future events. Nonlinear Hawkes models are a popular choice for examining these relationships and have been extended to include persistent connections between events and their own derivatives. Despite the benefits of Bayesian estimation, particularly in the absence of large data sets, the computational challenges associated with their implementation have limited its use. To address this issue, a new efficient method based on the use of adjoint methods and Euler scheme has been developed in the course of this research and is being made available to the public. This method provides significant improvements in the speed of calculation and accuracy, allowing for the Bayesian estimation of Bayesian nonlinear Hawkes models through the use of the Euler scheme.

Within intense laser-plasma interactions, the polarization state can shift at an incredible pace, leading to polarization transformation and possible ramping to unprecedented levels. We introduce a new rapid cross-polarization amplification mechanism caused by the angle-typed asymmetry of the plasma electron distribution, which can reach spectacular degrees of polarization enrgy transfer and result in the formation of extremely intense, purely linearly polarized laser pulses. This theoretical model is validated by conducting relevant particle-in-cell simulations and provides insights for realizing linearly polarized high-power laser systems through proper adjustment of magnetic fields in plasma.

Revisiting the estimation of the tau lepton's electric dipole form factor, we calculate its leading contribution within the standard model, both in the on-shell and $\overline{\text{MS}}$ schemes. Furthermore, corrections arising from the incorporation of the weak interaction, finite size effects, and the influence of light quarks and leptons are evaluated. Utilizing these inputs, we provide updates to the estimation of the tau lepton's electric dipole moment, including an assessment of theoretical uncertainties.

We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of symmetric errors, and our analysis reveals that the list size of decodable codes can be significantly reduced compared to their error-free counterparts while maintaining their error-correcting capabilities. In particular, we show that for code rates greater than 1, there exist codes that can correct up to half the maximum rank of the identity matrix and whose list size is one for any possible error matrix. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that for code rates less than 1, there are codes that can correct up to the maximum rank of the identity matrix and whose list size is one for any possible error matrix, thus surpassing the limit imposed by the Singleton rank distance bound.

Building upon the fundamental comprehension of the operator product expansion in CFT$_2$, we provide a concise analysis of its analog in AdS$_3$. In particular, we examine the properties of spinning conformal primary operators that constitute the operator product expansion, with a focus on the mode functions and wave operators in both the bulk and boundary descriptions. By equating the AdS$_2$ mode functions to specific two-point conformal block expressions, we derive an invariant two-point correlation function in the operator product expansion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that spinning descendant operators in the operator product expansion can be characterized by descendant conformal partial wave operators in the bulk AdS$_3$ cross-ratio, with implications for the operator product expansion in CFT$_2$.

In 1976, Gelfand and MacPherson established that the Pontrjagin classes of a manifold can be calculated using a polynomial ring with coefficients in rational functions. We provide a new proof of this theory, also showing that the coefficients of these classes are related to the minors of a specific submatrix of the Jacobian matrix of a generating function.

We analyzed the optical and near-infrared light curves and spectra of SN~2020jfo, a supernova exhibiting a rare and short luminosity plateau phase. By re-examining the light curves with a new method that removes systematic errors, we determined the duration of the plateau phase to be approximately 13 days. SN~2020jfo is only the second known Type II-S supernova within a sample of 160 Type II supernovae in a specific galaxy type group that has a short plateau duration. We also found that SN~2020jfo shares similar explosion and ejecta properties with the SN~1999gb, and that its light curves can be fit with a two-component model consisting of a standard Type II supernova component and a component resembling that of an extreme supernova. Furthermore, we propose an alternative explanation for the short plateau duration based on an extreme supernova interaction with a massive hydrogen-rich companion star in a galaxy with an elevated star formation rate.

To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray telescopes employing a lobster-eye lens array, we propose a novel concept where multiple lenses of varying focal length are used in a multiplexed configuration. By assigning shorter focal length lenses to the periphery of the detector and longer focal length lenses to the center, we show that an arrangement consisting of just 25 lenses can cover a field of view of up to 20 degrees in full frame mode. When a 4x4 pixel packet is used, this setup can accommodate up to 100 independent images per exposure within the same field of view. The proposed layout's effectiveness in reducing effects like saturation, transient events, and persistent gradients across the array is demonstrated, along with its ability to achieve high-time-resolution spectra in a broad-field mode of observation.

We investigate a type of partial elliptic operators, which we call'stage elliptic,' and demonstrate their utility in solving a nonlinear degenerate elliptic obstacle problem on a single domain and a bistable transition layer problem on the real line.

To explore the link between the structure of dark matter and cosmic velocity, our research leverages two sophisticated neural network models to analyze dark matter halo distributions within a vast universe model. Comparing their findings to actual universe data, our results show that the influence of velocity on halo formation is minimal, with an estimated effect of less than 1% when considering the mass of halos and their central regions. Conversely, velocity is found to have a more significant impact on the distribution of halos on the edges, with an estimated effect of around 5%.

We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars within the framework of general relativity. Our method uses a stress-energy tensor that includes radiation and matter components, with the former described using a conformally flat spacetime. By solving the Einstein field equations within this context, we are able to determine the metric of the spacetime surrounding the star. Our method has been tested by comparing numerical results to analytical solutions for non-rotating stars and rotating neutron stars in the limit of low rotation rates.

A major obstacle in creating AI models to automate document data extraction is the time and money required to accurately label large sets of documents. To overcome this challenge, a team of researchers from Hugging Face and the University of Colorado Denver explore the minimal amount of labeling necessary to effectively train a model for document data extraction. They concentrate on extracting financial information from invoices and conclude that with a targeted, activity-based labeling approach, it's possible to reduce labeling costs by 98% while still achieving comparable performance to more comprehensive labeling methods.

The vast parameter space of gravitational waves means that even with ongoing observations, the number of detectable signals will far exceed computational resources available for traditional matched-filtering methods used to identify signals from noise in gravitational wave data. To overcome this challenge, a new method was tested where a neural network was trained on signals from numerical simulations of neutron star-black hole mergers with 45 parameters, varying the properties of the neutron star and black hole. The network achieved a purity of 50% in identifying signals, and for recovered signals with signal-to-noise ratio 8 or higher, it yielded a 90% purity; it also accurately determined the mass ratio of the merged objects with an error of less than 0.05 and distinguished q=2 from q=4 with 95% confidence.

This research leverages mobile data from a large European city to Le Corbusier's concept of a "right to the city." Le Corbusier envisioned equal access to the city's amenities for all residents despite physical distance. Le Corbusier's metric Le Residu measures inequality in this context. It is calculated as the standard deviation of the number of amenities each resident has access to within their physical distance. In a significant shift from prior findings, we show that during the pandemic, this metric Le Residu decreased more slowly for the lower economic classes than for the higher economic classes. This research offers an interdisciplinary perspective, informed by urban economics, sociology, and geography. It provides an actionable, quantifiable method, form of Le Residu, to study inequality in urban interactions.

Three-dimensional simulations of massive young stars reveal their surrounding environments to be complex, with multiple clumps of material accumulating to form the star. These simulations indicate that massive stars form through the merger of several individual clumps with high masses, rather than a single massive accumulation. When these clumps collide, they release massive amounts of energy and radiative feedback, significantly impacting the surrounding gas. As a result, the formed star exhibits variations in mass and luminosity over time. Based on these findings, researchers suggest that massive stars may be binary or multiple star systems waiting to form, with the mergers occurring as they evolve.

This research develops a Hamiltonian Dysthe equation to model the long-wave limit of deep-water gravity waves with constant vorticity, as part of a wider effort to generalize the Dysthe equation to include effects of vorticity and surface tension. The Hamiltonian Dysthe equation is derived through a expansion approach, focusing on weak nonlinear effects and no limitation on primary wave amplitudes. The obtained equation includes terms representing the influence of vorticity and surface tension. To validate the obtained equation, simulations of an initial condition were conducted and the results compared to those obtained using a direct numerical simulation of the full Euler equations. The Hamiltonian Dysthe equation was also applied to a range of random wave fields with varying levels of vorticity and surface tension. The Hamiltonian Dysthe equation was found to perform well for random waves with an average wave amplitude less than 0.2 when comparing the wave spectrum to the results of direct numerical simulations.

A recently developed concept from analysis, "locally convex terrains," serves as the foundation for an original, expansive proof of the Stokes theorem within the framework of differential forms. This proof not only provides a distinct perspective on the theorem's classical interpretation but also offers a framework for generalizing it to suitable contexts in analysis. A key aspect of our approach involves demonstrating that locally convex terrains can be equipped with a differential structure that enables the application of classical differential geometry techniques. This is achieved by utilizing the terrains' topological characteristics to construct a differential structure, thereby ensuring that locally convex terrains are homeomorphic to spaces derived through the quotient of a Euclidean space by a specific set of transformations. A significant expansion upon the original proof is a rule for extending the Stokes theorem to the context of locally convex terrains, thereby expanding the theorem's domain of applicability.

Our method allows navigation systems with multiple frequencies to be
combined (blended) in real-time. This technique helps mitigate the risks
associated with signal loss, echolocation limitations, and malfunctions
in sonar devices. Our study focuses on a generic navigation system and
analyzes the combined signal's characteristics to determine its suitable
applications. Specifically, we examined the effects of signal frequencies,
orientation, device position, and beam patterns on the combined signal's
features. Our results reveal that certain frequency combinations can
effectively prevent signal loss and reduce the impact of signal distortions,
while others may create new problems with signal distortions or fail to
improve the situation with the lowest frequency. Our findings also indicate
that the best frequency combinations vary depending on the environment,
device configuration, and system settings. Ultimately, our analysis
demonstrates that the most advantageous frequency combinations depend on the
values obtained from feature extraction in each particular scenario.

The prevalence of deceptive news poses a significant challenge to society, with potentially far-reaching consequences. Social media platforms have struggled to effectively identify and remove this type of content, due in part to the risk of false positives and resulting legal repercussions. A key finding of our research reveals that summaries generated through automatic text summarization can serve as an reliable proxy for fraudulent news detection, with a notable improvement in accuracy. By leveraging pre-trained language models and neural network-based techniques, our proposed method achieves outstanding performance on two disparate and representative data sets, with notable gains in both model-based and rule-based evaluations. The former indicates that the model has gained significant insight from the training data, with a notable boost in accuracy when comparing to a baseline model. The latter reveals that our method conforms to expected patterns when evaluating fake news across various credibility levels.

We examine the behavior of a function f within a random field that has a specified characteristics, specifically in relation to the Gaussian model. This model is characterized by an inductive bias that is controlled by the specific characteristics of the random field, which results in the optimal function f being located within a specific subset of functions that are smooth and consistent across their entirety. We explore three defined random fields - polynomial fields, exponential fields, and the fields associated with the Mat\'ern model - each with their own distinct characteristics of behavior. We then provide a detailed analysis of the parameters of these random fields, specifically their bending parameters, which serve as a key component in understanding the inductive bias of each field. We go on to demonstrate how these parameters impact the inductive bias, which in turn affects the behavior of the optimal function f. Finally, we address the challenges faced in estimating the bending parameters of Gaussian process regression models.

We introduce a new algorithm to compute the principal component of a data matrix whose rows are subject to unknown rotations. This algorithm achieves linear convergence and is efficient for large datasets. We also establish a lower bound on the rate of convergence. To demonstrate its usefulness, we apply the algorithm to several synthetic and real-world problems involving shared and individual component analysis. In these examples, it significantly outperforms the current state-of-the-art method.

Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, due to the high expense and subjectivity of human annotation, such datasets remain limited. To compensate for this limitation, many research proposals have been made to leverage labeled data and neural language models in a semi-supervised learning framework. Semantic annotation revision is a method that falls under such proposals; it utilizes language models to revise annotations made by other individuals. Despite the benefits it affords, prior work has shown that standard annotation revision methods struggle to achieve satisfactory results when comparisons are made to other individuals. Building on this discovery, we developed a novel comparison-aware revision method that integrates the perspectives of original annotators and those of a BERT-based model. In our experimentation with a semantic annotation dataset centered on emotions, our method showed significant gains over the standard approach.

For mobile robots to navigate effectively in unfamiliar environments, having an efficient mapping strategy is crucial. Current mapping approaches primarily focus on direct representations, leading to performance optimization but potential complications when the environment changes. In contrast, our research introduces a novel navigation framework based on a unique hierarchical layout, the HiTMap, which condenses complex spatial information into simplified nodes and edges for localized determination. Unlike fixed mapping structures, HiTMap dynamically reorganizes itself in response to new data, fusing existing knowledge with fresh input to update the mapping seamlessly. By limiting search operations to localized areas, HiTMap ensures efficient path planning while minimizing the risk of getting trapped in an incorrect mapping branch. We have experimentally verified the efficacy of HiTMap, demonstrating notable improvements in navigation performance and mapping adaptability when compared to a leading, non-hierarchical SLAM implementation.

Our research employs interferometric techniques with neon-9 atoms to detect magnetic fields and test the Lorentz symmetry. By leveraging a neodymium magnetic field produced via a laser-powered process, we demonstrate enhanced detection capabilities and achieve a record-breaking symmetry coefficient of $R_{\gamma\gamma\phi}/R_{\gamma\gamma}\approx 1.15\times 10^{-5}$. Furthermore, we explore the possibility of utilizing a superconducting material's Meissner effect to create an escutcheon for improved field detection within atomic interferometry.

In this work, a mixture model consisting of non-identical components is reimagined using measures that elude the traditional non-negative constraint. measures that minimize distance to indicator measures of each component are proposed, resulting in a characterization of components as convex bodies within a fixed set of measures. Theoretical properties, such as consistency of estimator and sparsity, are maintained under certain conditions on the underlying measure space. A soft-identifier method based on the Wasserstein distance yields a linear representation of components as convex bodies, demonstrating the feasibility of recovering underlying structures. A numerical example showcasing the underlying geometry of mixtures also is presented.

High-performance computing on the SIMD architecture within GPUs is complicated 
by multiple ongoing threads competing for memory resources being managed by the 
memory allocator. Current memory allocators are not designed to handle this level 
of concurrency, leading to a significant bottleneck. Despite this challenge, developers 
have been using C++ and other object-oriented programming languages on the GPU 
with remarkable success, largely due to their ability to reduce programming errors 
and improve code scalability. To overcome the current memory allocator limitations, 
we present DynaSOAr, a concurrent memory allocator designed specifically for object-oriented 
programming on the GPU. DynaSOAr is engineered to minimize memory competition and 
efficiently manage memory usage across the GPU. We have further engineered DynaSOAr 
to incorporate advanced features such as real-time memory analysis, automatic memory 
correction, and optimized memory reuse. Our findings, obtained using real-world applications 
and N-body simulation benchmarks, demonstrate that DynaSOAr outperforms the current 
memory allocator by 1.5 times on the V100 GPU and 2 times on the A100 GPU.

A new approach to describing the spin-resolved levels of an impurity in a s-wave superconductor is proposed, with the aim of accurately accounting for both the electronics and spin dynamics within the system. Based on an initial principles calculation of the impurity's potential energy, the theory relies on a minimal number of assumptions and incorporates the results in a semi-analytical $T$-matrix formulation. When applied to an individual manganese adatom on niobium, the theory shows both agreement with and distinction from previous models. Furthermore, the theory is extended to an individual manganese adatom located at a step edge of the niobium surface and a dimer situated at a edge site.

K2 object TOI-712, located in the Scorpius-Centaurus complex, is scrutinized using data from Chilean telescope TRIS, Kepler space telescope, spectroscopic data from HARPS, and Euclid mock observations.  TOI-712 comprises a quartet of planets orbiting a G-type star and include two Earth-sized planets with rock and gas compositions and a pair of mini-Neptunes surrounding the star's habitable zone.  Earth-sized planets, named TOI-712.02 and TOI-712.03, possess orbital periods of 8.37 and 21.88 days while the mini-Neptunes, named TOI-712 d and TOI-712 e, have orbital periods of 38.86 and 47.4 days.  The team analyzed atmospheric retention using host star properties, planet interactions, and orbital elements and found that planets TOI-712.02, TOI-712.03, and TOI-712 e have atmospheric retention above 1% and that the Earth-sized planet TOI-712.04 has the highest retention rate of 50%.  Further research revealed that the planets' interactions influenced their retention levels and that the star exhibited little variability over the observation period.  Further analysis suggested that the system had 20 million years of age and included a misaligned mini-Neptune (TOI-712 e) with a high eccentricity of 0.32.

To explore the potential of carbon and nitrogen in enhancing the magnetic properties of titanium dioxide through doping, a computational study using density functional theory was conducted. Different doping arrangements, including substitutional, interstitial locations within the 1b$_{2g}$, 2b$_{2g}$, 4f$_{2g}$, and 3d$_{3z^2-r^2}$ orbitals, and their combinations were examined. The results showed that both elements can exhibit ferromagnetic behavior after doping, with the most desirable effects arising from the 1b$_{2g}$ and 3d$_{3z^2-r^2}$ orbital arrangements in their respective categories. However, their magnetic properties are highly dependent on the oxygen column distance, ranging from 2.88 to 2.99 \ Å, with the most stable arrangements occurring at the middle oxygen column distance range. A notable finding was that nitrogen doping exhibited greater stability compared to carbon doping, with more significant differences in bond lengths and lattice energies.

One of the key aspects of the Standard Model's completeness testing lies in examining the Standard Model's elastic scattering predictions within the Large Hadron Collider's data. To enhance the significance of these searches, we propose utilizing forward detectors like the CMS experiment's Roman Pulsar upgrade to search for the exclusive production of high-transverse-momentum elastic $t\bar{t}$ pairs, where the collision outcome is characterized by the presence of two jets and significant missing transverse energy. This novel analysis leverages specialized techniques that identify the scattering plane, leading to a signal-to-background discrimination of at least three orders of magnitude. As such, we believe this method will yield the first direct evidence of the elastic production of heavy quarks and provide a precise measurement of the $W$ boson's total cross-section at 13 TeV. Additionally, this analysis serves as a critical component in identifying forward-scattering events that mediate top quark pairs and contribute significantly to the total top quark cross-section.

An infinite graph is considered rich if it contains every possible substructure of a specified type. In the context of Ramsey theory, a key concept is combinatorial structure, which encompasses a broad range of substructures including triangles, four-cycles, cliques, and more. An infinite graph's richness can be determined by examining the individual components that make up the graph. Our research focuses on identifying Ramsey upper bounds for the richness of graphs with specific properties, including connectivity, local resilience, and the absence of particular substructures. Notably, we find that connected graphs have a higher upper bound for richness than isolated edges or cliques within the graph.

Our research builds upon the quantum analog model for scalar QED in (1+1)D, specifically the "sound meter" measurement, which detects and measures "sound" in the model's equilibrium state. We calculated the corrections to the metric that measures "sound" and identified its components, particularly the longitudinal component, which indicates the level of "sound" in the model. We obtained these results using both large-N and semi-classical approaches. Furthermore, we found that the long-wavelength corrections to the metric are proportional to N by calculating the "sound meter" metric in semi-classical approximation within the semi-classical large-N framework. We then explored the "sound meter" metric in semi-classical large-N framework for massless sQED within the semi-classical large-N framework and determined its components. We also determined the "sound meter" metric components for massive sQED within the semi-classical large-N framework along with its components. We then examined the "sound meter" metric within the semi-classical large-N framework for both massive and massless sQED and identified its components. We obtained the "sound meter" metric within the semi-classical large-N framework for both massive and massless sQED and explored its components. We explored the "sound meter" metric within the semi-classical large-N framework for both massive and massless sQED.
